articles.title: Lessons Learned: Wifi Server Disaster
articles.description: So there I was, figuring out how to set up all my social media for branded automated posting....
articles.body_html:
So there I was, figuring out how to set up all my social media for branded automated posting. Pinterest requires a privacy policy link to do certain things. No problem. I have that. Or at least I thought I did...

When I went to my site to grab the privacy policy link, it returned with some strange error I had never seen before. It was like 1003 or something like that. Complete and utter failure. Shocked, I reached for sentry (which I had been leaning on, of course) free tier used up. No more uptime monitoring enabled. I got too cozy. I go to the server, it's on and running, and appears functional. After some quick digging, I discovered it was wifi. The server was still running on wifi. I knew that, but I never experienced a disaster like this first hand.

Why is it on wifi, you ask? The original intention was for poking around, learning, and other activities not intended for a production server. 😂 it has snowballed into something with a tiny heartbeat. ****

Back to the why: it's sitting next to the switch that I have yet to configure. 2 switches actually. A juniper and a cisco. I am at a crossroads. The juniper would be free, but I was studying cisco. I started studying networking stuff but I've been very busy. And im not putting my desktop on wifi.

Want some sprinkles? The server is on the opposite side of the house, on a different floor, with lots of structure in between. I have 2 cat6a cables running down. We have about 25+ things that need internet, in that room alone. Have fun thinking about that.

Damnit! 😂 I wasn't ready yet! My plans have now changed. Tomorrow I attempt a network configuration. No one to hold my hand and walk me through the process here. Certain panic. Wish me luck.

My server that I have been working so hard on had an unplanned 2 hour outage while I updated it in a panic. This must be what it feels like to work in cybersecurity. Panic panic everywhere.

I have an actual big server (its old) but I haven't got it fully configured, and also I wanted my switch up. Its a big fat cycle of excuses. I can't continue like this. 😂😂😂

I guess I have to be a baby system admin now. This was not a part of my original plan. I swear I spend more time fixing problems (that I created) than anything else.

I fully updated my tiny server since it was already down, and turned off power saving. Its not enough, but if I'm lucky, I'll get a switch working tomorrow... maybe?

I also learned I need a redirect page for when my server is down for maintenence. Basic stuff if you think about it. I am but a single junior dev, don't shoot. XD

Side note: As I was explaining this to my significant other, first, his jaw dropped. Then, he busted out laughing because he said he was planning on "play with the wifi tomorrow." Then my jaw dropped.

Disasters.

Undoubtedly this should make for an interesting story, if nothing else.

articles.title: Shipping Flutter Web to Firebase When Your GitHub Actions Budget Hits Zero
articles.description: On October 18, right in the middle of shipping a multi-feature audit and a supplement tracker...
articles.body_html:
On October 18, right in the middle of shipping a multi-feature audit and a supplement tracker redesign on my personal life_os_app (my daily Flutter Web + Cloud Firestore operating board), GitHub Actions stopped scheduling jobs. The billing meter for my personal account's hosted runner minutes had hit 100%.

Look at what my .github/workflows/ci.yml and deploy-live.yml were doing on every push and pull request:

  1. Spinning up an ubuntu-latest VM.
  2. Pulling the Flutter SDK and warming the Pub cache (~90s).
  3. Installing Python 3 and running 68 CLI sync unit tests (~15s).
  4. Running flutter analyze and 466 widget and accessibility tests (~110s).
  5. Compiling flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn (~140s).
  6. Authenticating via Workload Identity Federation (google-github-actions/auth@v2) and deploying to Firebase Hosting target board (~35s).

That is 6.5 minutes per PR push and another 4 minutes on merge to main. Across 70+ PRs in October, a single-developer personal project burned through thousands of CI minutes doing work my local Apple Silicon MacBook finishes in under 30 seconds.

When your CI budget hits zero on a personal repo, the tempting fix is to move everything to your laptop, deploys included. I did exactly that when the budget ran out, and it taught me where the line belongs: verification moves to the laptop, the deploy stays in CI, and CI runs only when I ask it to.

Here is the exact architecture I use to keep life_os_app shipping to Firebase Hosting and Cloud Firestore while spending Actions minutes only on the builds that actually go live.

Architecture: The Three-Layer Local Verification Gate

Taking verification off the runners only works if nothing unverified ever reaches a deploy. In life_os_app, the application state is split across two runtimes:

  • Python 3.14 CLI Sync Tools (tool/board_*.py): Morning and evening scripts that pull from Apple Reminders, Google Calendar, Harvest, Notion, and GCP Billing, then write structured JSON documents into Cloud Firestore over REST.
  • Flutter Web Client (lib/): A Riverpod 3 + Material 3 multi-skin web app served from Firebase Hosting with a custom offline Service Worker (web/offline-sw.js).

Layer 1: Firestore Schema Validation Before Every REST Write

One of the biggest risks of running CLI sync tools outside a container is accidentally clobbering fields that the Flutter Web client writes directly from the browser. For example, on the Events and Admin tabs, I tick tasks directly in the UI (config/events.taskTicks and config/admin.done), while tool/board_events.py and tool/board_admin.py sync metadata from Notion and GCP Billing.

To prevent a CLI run from wiping browser taps, tool/board_firestore.py enforces two rules before any HTTP PATCH leaves the machine:

  1. Explicit schema validation on every collection (dayPlans, stats, config, finance, plan).
  2. Field-level update masks (?updateMask.fieldPaths=...) plus hard blocks against overwriting client-owned map keys: 
# tool/board_firestore.py
if path == "config/events" and "taskTicks" in data and not fields:
    raise SystemExit(
        "refusing to overwrite config/events.taskTicks without --fields; "
        "pass --fields updated,source,events"
    )
if path == "config/admin" and "done" in data and not fields:
    raise SystemExit(
        "refusing to overwrite config/admin.done without --fields"
    )

In addition, caching the gcloud auth print-access-token call with @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1) and enforcing a 15-second socket timeout cut multi-document Firestore sync latency by 80% and eliminated hanging background processes when switching Wi-Fi networks.

Layer 2: Per-Document Decode Isolation in Flutter Streams

In Cloud Firestore, a single malformed field inside one historical document in a collection query (collection('dayPlans').snapshots()) will normally throw a FormatException or TypeError inside .map(), killing the entire StreamProvider and replacing your UI with an error state.

During my audit pass, I hardened every repository to isolate decoding per document:

// lib/features/day_board/data/board_repository.dart
List<T> _decodeEach<T>(
  QuerySnapshot<JsonMap> query,
  T Function(JsonMap data, String id) decode,
) {
  final results = <T>[];
  for (final doc in query.docs) {
    try {
      results.add(decode(doc.data(), doc.id));
    } on Object catch (error, stackTrace) {
      developer.log(
        'Skipping malformed document ${doc.reference.path}',
        name: 'day_board.repository',
        error: error,
        stackTrace: stackTrace,
      );
    }
  }
  return results;
}

When saving multi-day edits (such as editing 7 days of focus blocks and habit notes in the This Week sheet), replacing 14 sequential await set() calls with a single atomic WriteBatch (saveWeekEditsBatch) eliminated partial-save race conditions on flaky mobile connections.

Layer 3: Self-Contained Web Bundles (--no-web-resources-cdn) & Service Worker Cleanup

When deploying Flutter Web to Firebase Hosting for daily use on iPhone, iPad, and desktop, CDN font/CanvasKit fetches can stall on airplane or train Wi-Fi. Building with --no-web-resources-cdn bundles CanvasKit and font assets directly into build/web/, paired with a custom web/offline-sw.js that races network against a 3.5-second timeout before falling back to cache:

// web/offline-sw.js
function networkFirst(request, timeoutMs) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timeout')), timeoutMs);
    fetch(request)
      .then((response) => {
        if (response && response.ok) {
          caches.open(CACHE).then((cache) => cache.put(request, response.clone()));
        }
        resolve(response);
      })
      .catch(reject)
      .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
  }).catch(() => caches.match(request));
}

Notice the .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer)) cleanup: without it, every fast network response leaves an orphan timer running until timeoutMs expires.

The Deploy Stays in CI, on Demand

While Actions was out of minutes, I shipped with firebase deploy --only hosting:board straight from my Mac, every time after running the full gate locally. It worked, and it stayed an emergency exit, not the new normal.

The reason is one file. lib/firebase_options.dart is gitignored: the real web config lives in the FIREBASE_OPTIONS_DART repository secret, and the deploy workflows write it into the checkout right before flutter build web. A local build depends on whatever copy of that file happens to sit on your disk. If it is stale or points at the wrong app, the bundle still builds and deploys, and Firebase web initialisation breaks for everyone who opens the board.

So the rule is: the laptop proves the code is good, CI builds and ships it. What changed is when CI runs:

# .github/workflows/ci.yml: pull requests only, docs and handoffs never trigger it
on:
  pull_request:
    paths-ignore: ['handoffs/**', 'my_life/**', 'docs/**', 'reviews/**', 'archive/**', '*.md']

# .github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml: by hand, any branch, to the staging site
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      ref: { description: Branch or commit to deploy, required: true, default: main }

# .github/workflows/deploy-live.yml: by hand, or a [deploy] marker in a commit on main
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

Plus a ~/.pub-cache cache keyed on pubspec.lock, cancel-in-progress on CI so a new push kills the stale run, and the Firestore rules emulator job gated to changes in firestore.rules or tool/**.

The minutes math changes completely. Before: about 6.5 minutes on every PR push and 4 more on every merge. Now: the local gate runs on every change for free, and Actions spends one build-and-deploy when I decide a batch of work is ready, usually once in the evening after I have tried it on staging.

Benchmarking: Cloud CI vs. Local Verification Gate

Stage GitHub Actions (ubuntu-latest) Local Apple Silicon Gate Improvement
Python CLI Unit Tests (68 tests) 14.2s (with setup) 0.02s 710x faster
Dart Format + Analyze + 466 Flutter tests 118.0s 14.5s 8.1x faster
flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn 142.0s 14.8s 9.6x faster
Total Wall-Clock Time ~4m 34s (plus SDK cache) ~29.3s ~9.4x faster, $0 CI cost

The deploy itself is not in the table on purpose: it runs in the workflow, once per release, not once per push.

Key Takeaways for Flutter & Firebase Engineers

  1. Keep CI YAML for PRs when budget allows, but make your local gate identical. A single local command (dart format -l 120 lib/ test/ && flutter analyze && python3 -m unittest discover -s tool -p '*_test.py' && flutter test) guarantees parity before you trigger a deploy.
  2. Verify locally, deploy from CI, and trigger deploys by hand. Secrets such as firebase_options.dart stay in one place, every live build is reproducible from a commit, and you pay runner minutes per release instead of per push.
  3. Use Firebase Hosting multi-site targets (hosting:board, hosting:staging). Mapping targets in .firebaserc lets you try a branch on staging, then promote to live, without touching sibling sites on the same GCP project.
  4. Never let one bad Firestore document take down a collection stream. Wrap per-document .fromJson() calls inside a helper that logs to dart:developer and skips the corrupted record.
  5. Test accessibility contrast and 44pt tap targets in flutter test, not in production. Running textContrastGuideline and androidTapTargetGuideline with GoogleFonts.config.allowRuntimeFetching = false catches neon text shadow contrast drops and 32pt icons in milliseconds.

The complete local gate in one command (the release build is in it, so a broken web build never reaches a workflow):

dart format -l 120 lib/ test/ && \
  flutter analyze && \
  python3 -m unittest discover -s tool -p '*_test.py' && \
  flutter test && \
  flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn

Then ship from CI, staging first:

gh workflow run "Deploy staging" -f ref=main

And once it looks right on your phone, live:

gh workflow run "Deploy live"

articles.title: AI wrote the first 90% of my app in an afternoon. The last 10% took three weeks.
articles.description: There's an old programmer's joke: the first 90% of the code takes 90% of the time, and the remaining...
articles.body_html:
There's an old programmer's joke: the first 90% of the code takes 90% of the time, and the remaining 10% takes the other 90% of the time. I used to tell it as a joke.

Then I let AI write a whole SaaS — auth, Stripe billing, a dashboard, a public API — and the joke stopped being funny. Because AI made the first 90% genuinely instant. And the second 90% was still exactly where it had always been, waiting for me, untouched.

The demo worked in an afternoon. The product took three more weeks. This is a field report on the gap between those two things — the part no demo ever shows you.

The first 90% really is solved

Let me be fair to the machine, because the first part was astonishing.

"Set up a Next.js app with Postgres and Drizzle, auth, a billing flow, a dashboard, and a public API." It did it. Correctly. In close to one shot. The scaffolding, the CRUD, the Zod schemas, the table with sorting and pagination — the stuff I actively dislike writing — came out clean, first try, no notes. By the end of day one I had something I could click through and demo to a friend. It looked done.

That's the trap. It looked done because everything that's easy to build is also easy to show. The demo path is the happy path, and the happy path is the 90% that was never the hard part.

The rule: the speed you feel in the first afternoon is real — and it's measuring the wrong thing. "I can demo it" and "it's done" are separated by the entire job.

The last 10% isn't code. It's anticipation.

Here's what the remaining three weeks were actually made of. None of it showed up in the demo, because the demo was one well-behaved user doing exactly what I expected.

  • The empty state. Day one, the dashboard has no data. The AI rendered a table with headers and a blank void underneath — technically correct, and it makes a brand-new user think the product is broken. There's no "add your first client" nudge, because I never asked for one, because in my head the table always had data in it.
  • The error state. The checkout worked perfectly — with a card that approves. The first time a real card got declined, the button just… hung. No message, no retry, no path forward. The AI built the road and no guardrail, because I'd only ever described the road.
  • The double-click. A user on a slow connection clicked "Subscribe" twice. Two Stripe subscriptions, one customer. The happy path fires once; real humans mash buttons.
  • The race. Same record open in two tabs, both saved. Last write wins, the other silently gone. Fine in a demo where one person clicks one thing at a time.
  • The 2am weirdo. A session that expired overnight, a stale dashboard left open, one click in the morning → a 401 the UI had no idea what to do with → white screen. "Handles a user doing something weird at 2am" is a different product from "handles me, awake, clicking in order."
  • The public API with no armor. No rate limiting. No stable pagination. No idempotency key on the POST, so a retried request quietly created the thing twice. All the behaviors that aren't features — they're the absence of disasters.

Every one of these compiled. Every one passed the happy-path test. Not one of them was in the demo. This is the last 10%, and it's made almost entirely of things you only know to build because you've been burned by their absence.

The first 90% is construction. The last 10% is anticipation. AI is extraordinary at the first and has none of the second.

Why the AI can't close the gap

It's tempting to say "the model just isn't good enough yet." That's not what I found. The model built every single one of those fixes correctly the moment I described them. "Add an empty state." "Handle a declined card." "Debounce the submit." "Add an idempotency key." Done, done, done, done — perfectly.

The problem was never that it couldn't write the code. The problem is that it builds exactly what you describe, and the last 10% is precisely the stuff you don't think to describe. It has no scar tissue. It has never been woken at 2am by the empty state it forgot. So it will cheerfully hand you a demo and call it done, and it will be right that it's done — for the one user it imagined, who is always you, awake, behaving.

The rule: the AI closes the gap the instant you point at it. Knowing where to point is the whole job — and knowing where to point is just a list of every edge case that ever hurt you.

The uncomfortable part

So here's what actually happened to the shape of the work.

The first 90% — the part that felt like engineering, the typing, the construction, the thing that looks like progress on a screen share — collapsed to near zero. What's left is the part that never looked like much: sitting there cold, asking "what happens if they do this instead?" over and over until you've imagined every stupid, hostile, half-asleep thing a stranger will do to your software.

That part didn't get faster. If anything it got more exposed, because AI stripped away the busywork that used to disguise how much of the real job it always was. We told ourselves building software was mostly typing. It was mostly anticipating; the typing just took long enough to hide that.

And that's the senior skill. Not syntax. Not "knows the framework." The ability to look at a working demo and feel, in your gut, the nineteen ways it'll break in front of a real person. You don't get that from a model. You get it from having shipped the empty state that made someone think your product was broken, once, and never forgetting.

What I actually changed

I didn't stop using AI — I let it write 100% of the first 90%, and I'd never scaffold by hand again. I changed where I spend my attention, and how I define "done":

  • "Demo works" is the start of the work, not the end. The afternoon it clicks through is day one. I now budget the real schedule around the 10%, because that's the 90%.
  • I write the edge cases down before I build, not after they bite. Empty, error, loading, double-click, concurrent, expired, retried. It's a checklist now, because the model will never volunteer it and I will never remember all of it under pressure.
  • The thing that writes the code is never the thing that decides it's done. A separate reviewer, prompted to break the diff — "what does a hostile, half-asleep user do here?" — catches the missing states the author waves right past, because the author's mental model is the happy path by construction.

Author writes it, a skeptic tries to break it, a human owns the call on whether it's actually finished. That separation is the only reason I can hand the typing to a machine and still ship something that survives contact with a real user. It's also how we build Xenition — our AI workspace: describe the tool you want in plain language and it builds and deploys the working app, real database and real URL. The describing is instant now. The deciding-what-to-describe is still the job, and it always will be.

Would I do it again?

In a heartbeat. The first 90% in an afternoon is not a gimmick — it's the biggest change to how I build in a decade, and I'm never giving it back.

But I'd walk in knowing what the demo is lying about. "It works" means it works for the user you imagined. The last 10% is the work of imagining the ones you didn't — and that was always the whole job. AI just took away everything that used to hide it.

articles.title: Your "use server" Functions Are Public HTTP Endpoints (And Middleware Won't Save You)
articles.description: Adding "use server" makes a TypeScript function look private, but it actually exposes a public HTTP POST endpoint. Learn the 3 mistakes that leave React and Next.js Server Actions vulnerable and how to fix them.
articles.body_html:
If you import a 'use server' function into a protected React component and pass it a typed TypeScript object, it looks and feels like a private, internal function call.

It isn't. Every exported 'use server' function in your codebase is compiled into a publicly reachable HTTP POST endpoint. Anyone with your action's identifier can invoke it directly from curl, Postman, or an automated script—with any JSON payload they want, completely bypassing your UI and often bypassing the authentication checks you thought were protecting it.

If your team treats Server Actions like regular TypeScript functions instead of public REST endpoints, your production app likely has an unauthenticated mutation or an authorization bug waiting to be discovered.

The Illusion: Why Developers Write Vulnerable Actions

Look at this common pattern in a modern Next.js App Router codebase:

// app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx (Protected by Layout)
import { requireAdminSession } from '@/lib/auth';
import { issueRefund } from '@/app/actions/billing';

export default async function BillingPage() {
  // ✅ The developer checks authentication in the Page or Layout
  const session = await requireAdminSession();

  return (
    <form action={async () => {
      'use server';
      await issueRefund({ invoiceId: 'inv_9921', amountCents: 5000 });
    }}>
      <button type="submit">Issue $50 Refund</button>
    </form>
  );
}

And here is the action file it imports:

// app/actions/billing.ts
'use server';

import { db } from '@/lib/db';

interface RefundInput {
  invoiceId: string;
  amountCents: number;
}

// ❌ CRITICAL VULNERABILITY: Publicly callable POST endpoint!
export async function issueRefund(input: RefundInput) {
  await db.invoices.update({
    where: { id: input.invoiceId },
    data: { status: 'REFUNDED', refundedAmount: input.amountCents },
  });

  return { success: true };
}

During code review, almost everyone approves this. The reasoning seems obvious:

  1. BillingPage calls requireAdminSession() before rendering the button.
  2. issueRefund requires a strongly typed RefundInput object.
  3. No API route (app/api/.../route.ts) was ever created.

Every single one of those assumptions fails at runtime.


The Golden Rule of Server Functions: Adding 'use server' does not create a private server helper. It instructs the bundler to register an HTTP POST handler backed by the React Flight protocol and assign it a public Next-Action hash.

Mistake #1: Assuming Layouts or Parent Pages Protect Server Actions

When a user navigates to /dashboard/billing, Next.js renders layout.tsx and page.tsx. If you placed your requireAdminSession() check inside layout.tsx, unauthenticated visitors get redirected before seeing the UI.

However, when a client invokes a Server Action, Next.js does not execute the parent layout.tsx rendering logic as an authorization gate before running the action. A Server Action is an independent entry point.

Furthermore, relying solely on edge middleware (middleware.ts or proxy.ts in Next.js 16) is an anti-pattern. Edge routing layers are designed for optimistic redirects and request shaping—not as your sole data-access security boundary. Even if your middleware blocks /dashboard/*, a Server Action can be POSTed to any route in your application that accepts POST requests if the attacker sends the Next-Action header, or if matcher rules miss an unprotected path.

How an attacker triggers a "use server" function with curl
When your client bundle loads, the hashed action IDs are embedded right inside the JavaScript chunks served to the browser. Anyone inspecting the network tab or static JS files can grab the 40-character Next-Action hash and send a raw HTTP request:
curl -X POST https://your-app.com/login \
  -H "Accept: text/x-component" \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8" \
  -H "Next-Action: 409a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a" \
  -d '[{"invoiceId":"inv_9921","amountCents":9999999}]'

Notice that the request targets /login (a public route) while passing the Next-Action header for issueRefund. Without an explicit session check inside issueRefund itself, the database mutation executes immediately.


Mistake #2: Trusting TypeScript Types at Runtime

In our vulnerable issueRefund(input: RefundInput) example, the developer typed amountCents: number.

TypeScript types are completely erased during compilation. When an HTTP request hits a Server Action endpoint, the React Server Components (RSC) Flight deserializer parses the raw request body and passes whatever the caller sent directly into your function's arguments.

An attacker can send:

  • Negative numbers ({"amountCents": -500000})
  • Unexpected types ({"invoiceId": {"$ne": null}, "amountCents": "NaN"})
  • Massive multi-megabyte strings designed to block your event loop or bloat database columns

Even worse, framework-level deserialization bugs—such as the critical CVE-2025-55182 (CVSS 10.0) in React Server Components and CVE-2025-66478 in Next.js, followed by the May 2026 Flight parser DoS advisories—proved that Server Function endpoints sit directly on the untrusted network perimeter.

Mistake #3: Accidental Export Exposure in "use server" Files

When you put 'use server' at the top of a file (app/actions/users.ts), every single export in that file becomes a public HTTP endpoint—even internal helper functions you only exported so you could unit-test them or call them from another server file!

// app/actions/users.ts
'use server';

// ❌ You exported this only for a unit test or another server module,
// but because the file has 'use server' at the top, this is now a public endpoint!
export async function dangerouslyResetUserQuota(userId: string) {
  await db.quotas.update({ where: { userId }, data: { used: 0 } });
}

If a function does not need to be invoked directly from a Client Component or HTML <form>, never export it from a 'use server' file. Move shared server logic into a plain .ts Data Access Layer (DAL) marked with import 'server-only'.

The Production Fix: Harden Every Action Boundary

To make Server Actions safe in production, treat every 'use server' function exactly like a public POST /api/* webhook. Every action must enforce three rules inside its own body:

  1. Authenticate inside the action (never trust layouts or middleware).
  2. Validate the runtime payload with a schema (such as Zod or Valibot) using unknown as the TypeScript parameter type.
  3. Verify resource ownership (Authorization / IDOR check) before mutating data.

Here is the hardened, production-ready pattern:

// app/actions/billing.ts
'use server';

import { z } from 'zod';
import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import { getVerifiedSession } from '@/lib/dal/auth';

// 1. Define a strict runtime validation schema
const RefundSchema = z.object({
  invoiceId: z.string().uuid(),
  amountCents: z.number().int().positive().max(100_000_00),
});

// 2. Type the input as `unknown` so TypeScript forces you to parse it first
export async function issueRefund(rawInput: unknown) {
  // Step A: Authenticate inside the action itself
  const session = await getVerifiedSession();
  if (!session || session.user.role !== 'BILLING_ADMIN') {
    throw new Error('Unauthorized');
  }

  // Step B: Validate runtime types and constraints
  const parsed = RefundSchema.safeParse(rawInput);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { ok: false, error: 'Invalid refund payload' };
  }

  const { invoiceId, amountCents } = parsed.data;

  // Step C: Enforce tenant/object ownership (Prevent IDOR)
  const updated = await db.invoices.updateMany({
    where: {
      id: invoiceId,
      organizationId: session.user.organizationId, // Scope to caller's org!
      status: 'PAID',
    },
    data: {
      status: 'REFUNDED',
      refundedAmount: amountCents,
    },
  });

  if (updated.count === 0) {
    return { ok: false, error: 'Invoice not found or not eligible' };
  }

  return { ok: true };
}

Read the Official Next.js Data Security and Server Actions Architecture Guide

Quick Production Audit Checklist

Run through this checklist on your repository today:

  • [ ] Search your codebase for 'use server' and inspect every export async function.
  • [ ] Remove export from any helper function inside a 'use server' file that shouldn't be callable from the browser, or move it to a server-only Data Access Layer.
  • [ ] Ensure every exported Server Action calls your session/authentication verification inside its own function body.
  • [ ] Replace trusted TypeScript parameter types with rawInput: unknown + runtime schema parsing (zod or valibot).
  • [ ] Scope every database UPDATE and DELETE query by the authenticated user's userId or organizationId to prevent IDOR.
  • [ ] Keep react, react-dom, and next patched against React Flight protocol advisories (such as CVE-2025-55182 and CVE-2026-23870) and enforce request body size limits at your reverse proxy or WAF.

The Takeaway

The ergonomics of React Server Actions are their greatest strength and their biggest security trap. By erasing the visual boundary between client code and server execution, 'use server' makes network boundaries invisible.

Never assume a layout, middleware redirect, or TypeScript interface protects a Server Action. If a file says 'use server', every exported function is a public HTTP endpoint—authenticate it, validate its payload at runtime, and authorize every database query inside the action itself.

Have you audited the 'use server' files in your production codebase recently—and did you find any exported functions missing an internal auth or schema check?

articles.title: TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface
articles.description: Modern tuple types deliver position-based safety, labeled elements for IDE clarity, and variadic spreads for function composition. Learn when tuples beat interfaces and when to walk away.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most TypeScript engineers reach for interfaces when they need structured data. That reflex breaks when an API returns coordinates, a useState hook returns [value, setter], or middleware needs to compose through a chain of handlers. Arrays do not enforce length or per-index types. Interfaces force named property access when destructuring is cleaner.

The type system accepts [string, number] as valid but offers no hints at the call site. Engineers write result[0] with no indication whether zero holds a user ID or an error message. The compiler stays silent when position assumptions drift.

Labeled tuple elements fix this. The syntax [id: string, count: number] preserves position semantics while surfacing parameter names in autocomplete and signature help. Variadic tuple types compose middleware signatures. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The mechanics have been in TypeScript since 4.0 (August 2020) with variadic tuples and 4.2 (February 2021) with leading/trailing rest elements, per the TypeScript 4.0 release notes and 4.2 release notes. By 2026 the patterns are stable. What remains is knowing when a tuple wins over an interface and when adding a fourth element means you picked the wrong tool.

Key Takeaways

  • Labeled tuple elements [id: string, count: number] surface parameter names in IDE autocomplete and signature help with zero runtime cost.
  • Variadic tuple types enable type-safe function composition and middleware pipelines by spreading rest parameters into tuple positions.
  • Tuples beat interfaces when destructuring order matters, when position carries semantic meaning, or when returning small fixed-length collections from functions.
  • Readonly tuples and as const assertions prevent runtime mutations and lock down literal types at compile time.
  • Long tuples (more than 4 elements) sacrifice readability; switch to an interface when named properties clarify intent better than position.

What Makes TypeScript Tuples Different From Arrays in 2026

A tuple enforces fixed length and per-index types; an array enforces element homogeneity across unknown length.

An array of numbers number[] accepts zero elements or a million. The type system cannot tell you what lives at index three. A tuple [string, number, boolean] must hold exactly three elements with those exact types at those exact positions.

// Array: homogeneous, variable length
const scores: number[] = [42, 97, 88];
scores.push(103); // valid
const first = scores[0]; // type: number | undefined

// Tuple: heterogeneous, fixed length
const user: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
user.push(true); // error: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | number'
const name = user[0]; // type: string (exact)

The array allows mutation and length changes. The tuple enforces structure. When an API returns a latitude/longitude pair, [number, number] guarantees two elements. number[] leaves the consumer guessing whether the array holds two values or twenty.

Tuples compose with union types. A function returning [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] models a result type with discriminated positions. The caller destructures and checks the second element to know whether the first element is valid.

function fetchUser(id: string): [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] {
  // implementation
}

const [data, error] = fetchUser("123");
if (error) {
  console.error(error.message);
} else {
  console.log(data.name); // TypeScript knows data is User here
}

Arrays do not support this pattern. The type system cannot track which index holds the discriminant and which holds the payload. Tuples give you that precision.

TypeScript tuple type checking in IDE

Labeled Tuple Elements: Self-Documenting Types That Show Up in Your IDE

Labeled elements annotate each position with a parameter name, surfacing that name in IDE tooltips and autocomplete without changing the runtime shape.

The syntax [x: number, y: number] looks like a function signature. That is deliberate. When you destructure const [x, y] = getCoordinates(), the IDE shows those labels in the autocomplete list. The compiler still enforces position, not property access.

// Without labels
type Unlabeled = [number, number];
const point: Unlabeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const point: [number, number]

// With labels
type Labeled = [x: number, y: number];
const labeledPoint: Labeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const labeledPoint: [x: number, y: number]
// Destructuring autocomplete suggests 'x' and 'y'

Labels do not change destructuring semantics. You can still write const [a, b] = labeledPoint and a will hold the first element. Labels serve documentation, not enforcement. The compiler does not reject const [latitude, longitude] = labeledPoint even though the labels say x and y.

The real payoff comes in function signatures. A handler accepting (event: [type: string, payload: unknown]) => void shows those labels when you hover over the parameter. Compare that to (event: [string, unknown]) => void, which forces the reader to guess what the second element represents.

Labeled tuples pair well with utility types. A tuple [id: string, count: number] passed to Readonly<[id: string, count: number]> preserves labels while preventing mutation. The labels survive through type transformations.

Per the TypeScript 4.0 handbook on labeled tuple elements, labels must appear on all elements or none. Mixing labeled and unlabeled positions within the same tuple triggers a compiler error. Consistency keeps the intent clear.

Variadic Tuple Types: Composing Function Signatures and Middleware Pipelines

Variadic tuples spread rest parameters into fixed positions, enabling type-safe function composition and middleware stacks without manual overload declarations.

Before variadic tuples, composing two functions meant writing overloads for every arity. A pipe utility accepting (a: A) => B and (b: B) => C could not infer types for a third function without another overload. Variadic tuples solve this with spreads.

// A compose function that preserves types
type Fn<T extends unknown[], R> = (...args: T) => R;

function compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(
  f: Fn<A, B>,
  g: Fn<[B], C>
): Fn<A, C> {
  return (...args: A) => g(f(...args));
}

const addOne = (x: number) => x + 1;
const toString = (n: number) => n.toString();

const addThenStringify = compose(addOne, toString);
const result = addThenStringify(5); // type: string, value: "6"

The A extends unknown[] parameter captures the first function's argument tuple. The return type Fn<A, C> spreads that same tuple into the composed function's signature. TypeScript infers A as [number] when you pass addOne, then enforces that the composed function accepts number.

Middleware pipelines benefit more. An HTTP handler chain starts with [req: Request, res: Response] and each middleware adds context. Variadic tuples let you compose handlers that append parameters without losing type safety.

type Handler<T extends unknown[]> = (...args: T) => void | Promise<void>;

function withAuth<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    // auth logic
    return next(...args);
  };
}

function withLogging<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    console.log(req.url);
    return next(...args);
  };
}

const baseHandler: Handler<[Request, Response]> = (req, res) => {
  res.send("OK");
};

const protected = withAuth(withLogging(baseHandler));
// Type inferred: Handler<[Request, Response]>

The T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]] constraint preserves the leading two elements and allows trailing additions. Each middleware wraps the next without breaking the type chain. The final handler still accepts [Request, Response].

Variadic tuples also model Promise.all correctly. The built-in Promise.all<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: T): Promise<{ [K in keyof T]: Awaited<T[K]> }> uses variadic spreads to map each promise to its resolved type. You get Promise<[string, number]> from Promise.all([Promise.resolve("a"), Promise.resolve(1)]) instead of Promise<(string | number)[]>.

When a Tuple Beats an Interface: Position, Destructuring, and Performance

Tuples win when position carries meaning, destructuring is idiomatic, or the structure is small and temporary.

An interface forces named property access. A tuple lets you destructure in the parameter list or assignment. When a hook returns [state, setState], destructuring is idiomatic. Forcing { state, setState } adds noise.

// Tuple: destructure at call site
function useCounter(): [count: number, increment: () => void] {
  // implementation
}
const [count, increment] = useCounter();

// Interface: named access
interface CounterResult {
  count: number;
  increment: () => void;
}
function useCounterObj(): CounterResult {
  // implementation
}
const { count, increment } = useCounterObj();

Both work. The tuple version mirrors React's useState convention. The interface version clarifies when return values exceed two or three fields. Pick based on idiom and size.

Criterion Tuple Interface
Element count 2-4 elements 4+ fields
Destructuring const [a, b] = fn() const { a, b } = fn()
Property renaming Position-based, rename freely Must match property names or use alias
Documentation Labels in IDE, position implicit Property names explicit
Type overhead No keys, direct access Property lookup, structural check
Extension Cannot add optional trailing elements Can extend with optional properties

Tuples avoid property name collisions. When merging two results, destructuring with different names is trivial: const [user, setUser] = useUser(); const [post, setPost] = usePost();. Interfaces require renaming: const { data: userData } = fetchUser(); const { data: postData } = fetchPost();.

Performance differences are negligible. Both compile to arrays or objects. Tuples carry less metadata at runtime (no property keys), but modern engines optimize both paths. Choose based on semantics, not speed.

Tuples also model discriminated unions compactly. A result type [ok: true, data: T] | [ok: false, error: Error] discriminates on the first element. Interfaces would need a separate status field and duplicate the discriminant check.

Readonly Tuples and as const: Preventing Mutations at Compile Time

Readonly tuples block push, pop, and index assignment; as const assertions lock down literal types and infer readonly tuples automatically.

A bare tuple [string, number] allows mutation. The compiler accepts tuple[0] = "new value" and tuple.push(42) (though push violates the fixed length, the runtime allows it). Wrapping in Readonly<...> or using readonly [string, number] prevents both.

// Mutable tuple
const mutable: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
mutable[0] = "Bob"; // allowed
mutable.push(100); // runtime error, but TypeScript allows it

// Readonly tuple
const immutable: readonly [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
immutable[0] = "Bob"; // error: Index signature in type 'readonly [string, number]' only permits reading
immutable.push(100); // error: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly [string, number]'

The readonly modifier removes push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, and index assignment. The tuple becomes a pure value. Functions accepting readonly [string, number] signal they will not mutate the input.

The as const assertion infers readonly tuples and narrows literals to their exact values. Without it, TypeScript widens ["Alice", 29] to (string | number)[]. With it, the type becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with literal types.

// Without as const
const widened = ["Alice", 29]; // type: (string | number)[]

// With as const
const narrowed = ["Alice", 29] as const; // type: readonly ["Alice", 29]
const name = narrowed[0]; // type: "Alice" (literal)
const age = narrowed[1]; // type: 29 (literal)

This pairs well with exhaustive checks. A tuple ["success", "error", "pending"] as const gives you a union "success" | "error" | "pending" when spread. The compiler ensures switch statements cover all three cases.

const statuses = ["success", "error", "pending"] as const;
type Status = typeof statuses[number]; // "success" | "error" | "pending"

function handleStatus(status: Status) {
  switch (status) {
    case "success":
      return "OK";
    case "error":
      return "Failed";
    case "pending":
      return "Loading";
    default:
      const _exhaustive: never = status; // compiler error if a case is missing
      return _exhaustive;
  }
}

Readonly tuples prevent a class of bugs where shared state mutates unexpectedly. When a function returns readonly [User, Metadata], callers cannot accidentally modify the cached result. The type system enforces immutability without defensive copying.

Per the TypeScript handbook on const assertions, as const applies recursively. A nested tuple [["a", 1], ["b", 2]] as const becomes readonly [readonly ["a", 1], readonly ["b", 2]]. All layers lock down.

TypeScript readonly tuple preventing mutations

Real-World Patterns: API Returns, Event Handlers, and Multi-Value State

Tuples model API results with error/data pairs, event payloads with type and data, and stateful hooks returning value and setter.

A common pattern wraps API calls in a result tuple. The first element holds data on success, null on error. The second element holds the error or null. Destructuring gives immediate access to both.

async function fetchUserSafe(id: string): Promise<[data: User | null, error: Error | null]> {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    const user = await response.json();
    return [user, null];
  } catch (err) {
    return [null, err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(String(err))];
  }
}

const [user, error] = await fetchUserSafe("123");
if (error) {
  console.error("Failed to fetch user:", error.message);
} else {
  console.log("User:", user.name);
}

The caller checks the error element first. If null, the data element is safe to use. If present, the data element is null. The type system enforces this through union narrowing. No try/catch block needed at the call site.

Event handlers in frameworks like Svelte or custom event systems use tuples to pair event type with payload. A handler signature (event: [type: "click", target: HTMLElement]) => void documents both fields.

type ClickEvent = [type: "click", target: HTMLElement];
type KeyEvent = [type: "keydown", key: string];
type AppEvent = ClickEvent | KeyEvent;

function handleEvent(event: AppEvent) {
  const [type, payload] = event;
  if (type === "click") {
    console.log("Clicked:", payload.tagName);
  } else {
    console.log("Key pressed:", payload);
  }
}

The discriminant lives in the first position. TypeScript narrows payload based on type. A union of labeled tuples models tagged unions compactly.

Stateful hooks return tuples to mirror React conventions. A custom useToggle hook returns [value: boolean, toggle: () => void]. The caller destructures with meaningful names: const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle(false).

function useToggle(initial: boolean): [value: boolean, toggle: () => void] {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = () => setValue(v => !v);
  return [value, toggle];
}

Tuples keep the return compact. An interface would force { value, toggle }, which adds boilerplate. The tuple version reads cleaner when composing multiple hooks in a component.

For more on validating complex structures, see our guide on TypeScript form validators and custom validation logic, which covers zod and yup integration.

Common Pitfalls: Long Tuples, Type Inference Traps, and When to Use Objects Instead

Tuples lose clarity beyond four elements, inference fails when types are too similar, and objects win when order is arbitrary.

A tuple with six elements becomes unreadable. [string, number, boolean, string, Date, null] forces the reader to count positions. Named properties clarify intent faster than position.

// Bad: long tuple
type UserData = [id: string, name: string, age: number, email: string, createdAt: Date, deletedAt: Date | null];

// Better: interface
interface UserData {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  age: number;
  email: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  deletedAt: Date | null;
}

The interface version documents each field. The tuple version hides meaning behind indices. When you need more than four elements, switch to an object.

Type inference struggles when adjacent elements share types. A function returning [string, string] gives no hint which string holds the user ID and which holds the display name. Labels help, but the compiler cannot enforce destructuring order.

function getUser(): [id: string, name: string] {
  return ["u123", "Alice"];
}

const [name, id] = getUser(); // swapped, but compiler allows it

The destructured variables have the right types (both string), but the semantics are wrong. The compiler cannot catch this. When adjacent elements share types, consider an interface or an object with distinct keys.

Optional trailing elements create inference ambiguity. A tuple [string, number?] can hold one or two elements. Destructuring const [a, b] = tuple gives a: string and b: number | undefined, but you cannot tell from the type whether the tuple had one element or two.

type OptionalTuple = [name: string, age?: number];

const single: OptionalTuple = ["Alice"];
const double: OptionalTuple = ["Bob", 30];

const [name1, age1] = single; // age1: number | undefined
const [name2, age2] = double; // age2: number | undefined

The type system cannot distinguish at the call site. If the presence of the second element matters, model it as a discriminated union: [name: string] | [name: string, age: number].

Tuples also fail when order is arbitrary. A coordinate pair [x: number, y: number] has semantic order (horizontal, vertical). A user record with [email: string, phone: string] does not. Which comes first is a convention, not a constraint. Use an interface when order is arbitrary.

For a deeper dive into advanced type constraints, see our post on TypeScript generic constraints with extends and keyof.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should you use a labeled tuple instead of an interface?

Use a labeled tuple when the structure has 2-4 elements with semantic position order and the consumer will destructure it. Examples include coordinate pairs [x: number, y: number], React hook returns [state: T, setState: (val: T) => void], or result tuples [data: T | null, error: Error | null]. Use an interface when the structure exceeds four fields, when property names clarify intent better than position, or when order is arbitrary.

How do variadic tuple types improve function composition?

Variadic tuple types spread rest parameters into fixed positions, letting you compose functions without manual overloads. A compose utility can preserve the first function's argument tuple through type inference: compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(f: (...args: A) => B, g: (b: B) => C): (...args: A) => C. The type system infers A from the first function and applies it to the composed result, maintaining type safety across the chain.

What happens when you use as const on a tuple literal?

The as const assertion infers a readonly tuple with literal types for each element. ["Alice", 29] as const becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with types "Alice" and 29 instead of string and number. The readonly modifier prevents mutation, and the literal types enable exhaustive checking in discriminated unions. The assertion applies recursively to nested structures.

Can you extend a tuple type with additional elements?

TypeScript supports optional trailing elements with ? syntax: [required: string, optional?: number]. You cannot extend a named tuple type with inheritance the way you extend interfaces. Variadic tuple types allow composition: type Extended<T extends unknown[]> = [...T, extra: boolean] appends an element to the end. For dynamic extension, use rest elements: [first: string, ...rest: number[]].

When does a tuple perform better than an interface?

Tuples and interfaces both compile to runtime arrays or objects, and modern JavaScript engines optimize both paths aggressively. Tuples carry slightly less metadata (no property keys), but the performance difference is negligible in practice. Choose tuples for semantic reasons (position matters, destructuring is idiomatic) rather than performance. Microbenchmarks may show tiny differences, but they vanish under real workload variance.

Tuples in 2026: What You Should Reach For and When to Walk Away

Tuples deliver position-based type safety when destructuring is idiomatic and structure is small. Labeled elements clarify intent without runtime cost. Variadic spreads compose function signatures cleanly. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The pattern breaks at five elements. When property names clarify better than position, an interface wins. When adjacent elements share types, the compiler cannot catch swapped destructuring. When order is arbitrary, forcing a tuple sacrifices clarity for no gain.

Reach for tuples when returning small fixed-length collections from functions, modeling discriminated unions compactly, or composing middleware pipelines. Walk away when the structure grows past four fields, when naming beats numbering, or when the caller does not destructure. The type system gives you both tools. Use the one that documents intent.

For further refinement of type utilities, explore our coverage of Partial, Required, and DeepPartial patterns in TypeScript.

articles.title: We instrumented 11 production agents with real token accounting. In 9 of them, the most expensive step wasn't the model.
