articles.body_html:
Last quarter we finally stopped trusting the LLM bill. We wired real per-step token attribution into 11 production agents — not the default "total tokens" the provider hands you, but a tracer that tags every call, every tool, every cache lookup with the trajectory it belonged to.

The number that broke our mental model:

Across those 11 agents, the single most expensive step — measured per resolved task, not per API call — was the model in exactly 2 of them. In the other 9, something we'd filed under "negligible overhead" was quietly eating more than the LLM.

Here is the trap, in one picture. Same agent, same steps — two ways of ranking them.

WHAT THE DASHBOARD SHOWS (per-call mean)        WHAT THE BILL ACTUALLY IS (per-trajectory total)
Step                  $/call     rank            Step                  $/task      rank
LLM completion        $0.0028     #1              PII / guardrail       $0.0042     #1
PII / guardrail       $0.00035    #4              Embedding loop        $0.0036     #2
Embedding (in loop)   $0.00002    #5              LLM completion        $0.0028     #3
Semantic-cache chk   $0.00090    #3              Semantic-cache chk   $0.0009     #4
Tool call             $0.00010    #2              Tool call             $0.0008     #5

Left column: what every dashboard reports. Right column: what one task actually costs. The model drops from #1 to #3. A step you pay two-hundredths of a cent per call becomes the #2 cost driver. The ranking is not the same list.

And across all 11 agents, the #1 cost step by trajectory-total:

#1 cost driver (per trajectory), across 11 production agents
Embedding / retrieval loop   ██████████  5 / 11
PII / guardrail model        ██████      3 / 11
Model (LLM)                  ████        2 / 11
Cache-verify model           ██          1 / 11

Nine of eleven. The model isn't even in the lead most of the time.

The hidden axis: mean-vs-trajectory

The reason dashboards mislead is structural. They report mean cost per call, because that's what one request easily exposes. But an agent step isn't called once — it's called inside loops, per chunk, per re-plan.

The real cost of a step is:

step_cost_per_task  =  calls_per_task  ×  cost_per_call

A step at $0.00002/call looks free on the mean chart. Call it 180 times in a retrieval loop and it's $0.0036/task — more than the LLM, which runs once. The "free" step wins by 28%, on exactly the hard tasks you care about.

The invisible cost axis is trajectory-total vs call-mean. Every dashboard I've seen only draws one of them.

Three cases we actually shipped

These aren't hypotheticals — they're line items from the 11 agents.

Case 1 — The "free" embedding step that wasn't.
We had a retrieval step the finance team literally labeled free in the cost model (embeddings at $0.00002/call). It lives inside the agent's re-planning loop, which on hard tasks re-retrieves up to 180 times. 180 × $0.00002 = $0.0036/task. The LLM completion, called once, is $0.0028. So the step we scored as zero out-costs the model by 28% — on every hard task, which is the only tasks that matter.

Case 2 — The cache hit that cost more than the miss.
Our semantic cache doesn't just return the cached answer on a hit. It runs a reranker plus a 70B "is this still relevant?" check, to avoid serving stale advice. That verification costs $0.0009. A genuine miss regenerates from the 8B model for $0.0006. So a hit — the thing caches exist to save you — costs 50% more than a miss, across the 40% of traffic that hits. We were paying a "savings" tax and calling it a win.

Case 3 — The guardrail that 4×'d the bill.
A PII-scrubber runs a 7B model on every message chunk before the LLM sees it: 12 chunks × $0.00035 = $0.0042/task. We added it for a compliance ask and never costed it per-trajectory. It became the #1 line item on 3 of the 11 agents. Removing it wasn't on the table — but routing it to a 0.5B model dropped it to $0.0003, a 14× cut, with no detectable quality change on our eval set.

How you should actually measure

The fix is almost never "pick a cheaper model." It's accounting per trajectory so the loop multiplier can't hide, then routing each step to the right-sized model. We sit in front of 25+ models behind one OpenAI-compatible gateway; the interesting savings came from moving the scrubber and the cache-verify down, not from swapping the completion.

Three changes that took an afternoon:

  1. Attribute every token to a trajectory_id, not a request. If you can't say what one task cost, you don't know your cost.
  2. Rank by total, sample real tasks. Pull N resolved tasks, sum per step, sort by total. The mean chart will lie to you; the total won't.
  3. Put a cost_per_resolved_task SLO in place. Alert on the trajectory, not the call.

A minimal version of what we run:

cost_attribution:
  unit: trajectory          # not 'request' and not 'call'
  trace_id: trajectory_id   # tag every step, tool, cache lookup
  rank_by: total_cost       # never mean_cost
  alert:
    metric: cost_per_resolved_task
    threshold_usd: 0.02
  exclude_steps: []         # never exclude the 'cheap' steps

And the five lines that surface the buried step:

from collections import defaultdict

def rank_steps_by_task(events):
    per_step = defaultdict(float)
    for e in events:
        per_step[e.step] += e.cost_usd          # already trajectory-attributed
    return sorted(per_step.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])

# prints the REAL ranking — usually not what your dashboard shows
for step, cost in rank_steps_by_task(events):
    print(f"{step:24} ${cost:.5f}")

The question I'll leave you with

The dashboards aren't lying. They're reporting the axis that's easiest to measure. We spent a year optimizing model choice while a loop multiplier and a "free" safety step ran away from us — invisible the whole time, because nothing on the screen was drawing the trajectory-total axis.

So: when you last looked at your agent's cost, were you ranking by what one call costs — or by what one task actually costs? Because those are not the same list.

What's the step you've been treating as free?

articles.title: console.log is a legitimate debugging tool
articles.description: I've used breakpoints, profilers, and all the fancy devtools. But when something breaks at 1 AM, my...
articles.body_html:
I've used breakpoints, profilers, and all the fancy devtools. But when something breaks at 1 AM, my first move is still:

console.log("here");
console.log("here 2");
console.log("WHY IS THIS UNDEFINED");

It's not pretty, but it works. Here's what I've noticed over time:

  • Writing a log forces me to state what I expect. To log a value, I first have to decide what it should be at that line.
  • It works everywhere. Every language, every stack, zero setup.
  • The bug often shows up while I'm typing the log. Half the time I find it before running anything.

Where it stops working

The rule I follow now: if I've added more than 5 logs, I'm guessing, not debugging.

At that point the logs have stopped answering questions and started adding noise. That's the moment to stop and step through the code with a real debugger, where I can inspect state, watch the call stack, and see exactly where the value changes.

Print debugging isn't the problem

Used on purpose, console.log is a fast way to test a hypothesis. The trouble starts when it replaces thinking.

Print debugging isn't the problem. Not knowing when to stop is.

articles.title: How to find and stop dev servers Claude Code and Codex left running
articles.description: You run npm run dev and Vite says Port 5173 is in use, trying another one.... You didn't start...
articles.body_html:
You run npm run dev and Vite says Port 5173 is in use, trying another one.... You didn't start anything on 5173. An agent did, an hour ago, to check a page. It said the page looked good and moved on. The server didn't.

Here's how to find it and stop it:

  • Find it: lsof -nP -iTCP:5173 -sTCP:LISTEN shows the process listening on the port. Drop the port number to list every listening process.
  • Stop it: kill <PID>. If it's still there a few seconds later, kill -9 <PID>.
  • Claude Code: /tasks lists the session's background tasks. Select one and press x to stop it.
  • Codex: /ps lists the session's background terminals, and /stop stops all of them.
  • Grok Build: /tasks or Ctrl+G shows background tasks. Press x on one to stop it.
  • The catch: a server started with & or nohup inside an ordinary command isn't a background task. None of those lists show it, and it keeps running after the session ends.

Why does it say port 5173 is already in use?

Because something is still listening on it. Dev servers pick a fixed default port: 5173 for Vite, 3000 for Next.js. When it's taken, both quietly move on. Vite tries the next free port and logs Port 5173 is in use, trying another one.... next dev does the same when you didn't set a port, and says Port 3000 is in use by process <pid>, using available port 3001 instead.

That's convenient once. With agents, it adds up. Each one that checks a page starts its own server, and the next one lands on 5174, then 5175. Your browser tab, a callback URL, or a proxy config still points at 5173, which is now serving yesterday's code.

To make Vite stop instead of drifting, set server.strictPort: true in vite.config, or run vite --strictPort. Then a leftover server shows up as an error the first time, not as a mystery an hour later.

Which process is holding the port?

Ask lsof for the process listening on it:

lsof -nP -iTCP:5173 -sTCP:LISTEN

COMMAND   PID   USER   FD   TYPE  DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
node    48213   you    21u  IPv6  0x...      0t0  TCP *:5173 (LISTEN)

-sTCP:LISTEN matters. Without it, lsof -i :5173 also lists every program connected to the port, your browser included. That's why the popular one-liner lsof -ti :5173 | xargs kill can kill your browser along with the server.

To see everything that's listening, leave out the port: lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN. macOS has a few listeners of its own, such as ControlCenter on 5000 and 7000 for AirPlay. Leave those alone.

Then look at where the process came from:

ps -o pid,ppid,lstart,command -p 48213
lsof -a -p 48213 -d cwd -Fn

The first line shows when it started and the full command. The second prints its working directory, which tells you the project. If the parent PID (PPID) is 1, the process that started it has already exited and launchd adopted it. That's what a forgotten background server usually looks like.

Did Claude Code or Codex start it?

The process tree can't tell you once the parent is gone. The environment can. Claude Code sets CLAUDECODE=1 and CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID in every command it runs, and Codex sets CODEX_THREAD_ID. A server inherits them, and they stay with it after its parent exits. On macOS, ps -E prints a process's environment along with its command:

ps -E -o command= -p 48213 | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(CLAUDECODE|CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID|CODEX_THREAD_ID)='

This loop lists every listening process an agent started, with its port, directory, and session:

for pid in $(lsof -tiTCP -sTCP:LISTEN | sort -u); do
  agent=$(ps -E -o command= -p "$pid" | tr ' ' '\n' |
    grep -E '^(CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID|CODEX_THREAD_ID)=' | head -1)
  [ -n "$agent" ] || continue
  port=$(lsof -nP -a -p "$pid" -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -Fn | sed -n 's/^n.*://p' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')
  dir=$(lsof -a -p "$pid" -d cwd -Fn | sed -n 's/^n//p')
  echo "$pid  port $port $(basename "$(ps -o comm= -p "$pid")")  $dir  $agent"
done

The session ID is the one claude --resume <id> and codex resume <id> take, so you can reopen the conversation that started the server and ask it what the server was for. ps -E shows the environment the process started with, and only for your own processes. That's all this needs. For Grok Build, use the working directory and the command.

How do I stop it without breaking anything?

Send it a normal terminate signal first:

kill 48213

A dev server catches this, closes its watcher and sockets, and exits. Check with the lsof line again. If it's still listening after a few seconds, force it:

kill -9 48213

Kill the process that's listening, not its parents. When node exits, the npm run dev above it exits too. Killing upward can hit the shell or the agent that's still running in another tab.

Avoid pkill node and killall node. They also stop every editor extension, language server, and MCP server written in Node, and any dev server you meant to keep.

How do Claude Code, Codex, and Grok stop their own background servers?

Each agent keeps a list of the background work it started, and each list has a stop control:

  • Claude Code: Claude starts a long command as a background task, and you can move a running command there with Ctrl+B. /tasks (also /bashes) lists them; select one and press x to stop it. Tasks stop when Claude Code exits, including processes that detached under setsid or timeout. If you send the session to the background with /background instead of exiting, they keep running there.
  • Codex: a command that keeps running after Codex stops waiting for it becomes a background terminal, and the footer says how many are running. /ps lists them and /stop stops all of them. Since 0.115, interrupting a turn with Ctrl+C or Esc doesn't stop them. Quitting doesn't always stop them: Codex can keep a session running in its local background service, for example when you leave a running turn with Run in background. Run /stop before you quit.
  • Grok Build: the agent runs commands in the background itself, and Ctrl+B sends a running one there. Ctrl+G or /tasks shows them; press x on one to stop it. Stopping a task ends its process group, but not descendants that detached with setsid or nohup.

These lists only know about what the agent started as background work.

Why do some servers outlive the session?

Because the agent didn't start them as background work. When it runs npm run dev & as an ordinary command, the command returns at once, the server is handed to launchd, and no task list ever shows it. Quitting the agent doesn't touch it. The same happens when a background task starts its own nohup … &. Claude Code then reports the task as completed, while the children keep running (issue #92399).

Even tracked work gets lost. In one Claude Code issue, a wrangler dev started as a background task kept running for two days at 89% CPU and 2.5 GB of memory after the user moved on. In another, a hung Python process ran for 136 minutes at 16 GB after the session's context was compacted. The user found it with ps aux. Codex users report background terminals that "run forever", too.

Sessions you didn't close count as well. A Claude Code session sent to the background, or a Codex turn left with Run in background, keeps its servers on purpose.

How do I stop agents leaving servers behind?

None of the three vendors publish a rule for this, but you can tell the agent in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md:

## Dev servers
- Start dev servers as a background task, never with `&`, `nohup`, or `setsid`.
- Use the project's fixed port and set it explicitly (`vite --strictPort`, `next dev --port 3000`). If the port is taken, tell me instead of picking another.
- Stop any server you started once you've finished checking it.

The first rule keeps the server in the task list, where quitting the agent stops it. The second turns a leftover server into an error you see right away. The third is a request, not a guarantee: a Codex issue reports background jobs left running even after the user said not to. So keep the lsof check around.

Can I see which Terminal started each server?

That's what the Servers section in PonyMux's Inspector does. For each Terminal it lists every port that a process started there is listening on, with the port and the process name. It doesn't matter whether the agent used a background task, &, or nohup. PonyMux marks each Terminal's processes when they start, and the mark stays after the parent exits.

  • Click a row to open the server in your browser.
  • Hover it to see when and in which directory it started, the processes that started it (claude › npm › node), and its command.
  • Click the trash button to stop it. PonyMux sends a terminate signal and forces it after 3 seconds. Your shell and the agent keep running.

When the agent exits, Servers moves up near the top of the Inspector, where a forgotten server is hard to miss. Moving a Terminal to the Trash or Archive stops everything running in it. Servers only covers processes started in PonyMux Terminals; for anything else, use lsof.

For the details, see Servers.

PonyMux is free for macOS: download it here.

articles.title: Find Your Next Apartment with Search API: A London and San Francisco Guide
articles.description: Day 27 of 30 Days of Search.           TL;DR   To build an apartment finder with the Valyu Python...
articles.body_html:
Day 27 of 30 Days of Search.

TL;DR

To build an apartment finder with the Valyu Python SDK, turn a renter's requirements into neighbourhood-specific searches with valyu.search(), retrieve rental pages with their source links, merge duplicate URLs, and review individual listings before shortlisting them. This tutorial builds a Python and Streamlit tool for London and San Francisco, including weekly-to-monthly rent conversion and a downloadable shortlist.

The finished tool lets you:

  • Search selected rental websites from one brief.
  • Read the returned evidence and open the original listing.
  • Enter the advertised rent and confirm the details that matter.
  • Download your research, notes and reviewed shortlist.

You'll need Python 3.11 or later, as required by the pinned Streamlit 1.66.1 release, and a Valyu API key. We use the official Valyu SDK for search; you don't need a separate language-model API key.

The apartment looks great. Then you read the listing.

You find a flat that seems to fit your budget. The photographs look good. The location looks promising.

Then you notice the price is per week, not per month.

Or you're looking in San Francisco, and the advertised price is an effective average after a move-in concession. The monthly base rent is higher. Another promising result is a room in a shared apartment, even though you need the whole place.

You now have tabs open across several websites and a notes app full of half-remembered addresses.

Let's build something that helps with that specific job: find rental pages worth investigating, keep the evidence together, and produce a shortlist you can use to arrange viewings.

We'll work through two searches. The budgets and neighbourhoods below are example inputs, not claims about market averages or guaranteed availability.

Requirement London example San Francisco example
Home Entire one-bedroom flat Entire one-bedroom apartment
Monthly base-rent ceiling £2,200 GBP $3,200 USD
Areas to investigate Stratford, Lewisham, Finsbury Park Inner Sunset, Inner Richmond, Bernal Heights
Example move-in date 1 December 2026 1 December 2026
Commute to check King's Cross Embarcadero
Another question Does the landlord accept a cat? What is the pet policy, including any extra charges?

The app lets you change these inputs. It defaults the move-in date to 30 days from the day you run it.

How does an apartment discovery tool work?

An apartment discovery tool converts a rental brief into searches across relevant websites, then collects the returned pages for review. Valyu Search API supplies ranked results with source URLs and extracted text. Your application manages the renter's requirements, duplicate URLs, price calculations, review state and shortlist.

A search result starts the investigation. The reviewed listing determines whether you should contact the advertiser.

Our first version has a simple path:

Rental brief
  → One web search per neighbourhood
  → Source-linked candidate pages
  → Listing review and rent normalization
  → Downloadable shortlist

For London, the source configuration includes OpenRent, Rightmove and Zoopla. For San Francisco, it includes Zillow, Apartments.com and the San Francisco Bay Area Craigslist domain. These are example web-search filters, not direct inventory integrations or a promise that every website will return accessible results.

Keep the vocabulary local. A London query should include “flat to rent”. A San Francisco query should include “apartment for rent” and the city name. Country targeting adds context, but the query still needs the city and neighbourhood.

Step 1: Set up the Python apartment finder

Create a project and install the Valyu SDK and Streamlit:

mkdir apartment-finder
cd apartment-finder
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install valyu==2.13.2 streamlit==1.66.1

Add a .gitignore before storing credentials:

.env*
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pem
*.key
credentials.*
secrets.*
shortlist-*.json

Set VALYU_API_KEY in the environment of the terminal that will run the app. In Bash or zsh on macOS or Linux, this reads the key without displaying it or putting its value in your shell history:

read -s VALYU_API_KEY
export VALYU_API_KEY

Paste the key at the prompt and press Enter. Keep it in the Python server process, not in browser JavaScript.

Step 2: Search rental websites with the Valyu SDK

The Valyu Python SDK reads VALYU_API_KEY automatically. Call valyu.search() with search_type="web" and the rental domains you want to investigate. The SDK handles the HTTP request and returns typed results.

Save this as first_search.py and run it with python first_search.py:

from valyu import Valyu

with Valyu() as valyu:
    response = valyu.search(
        "1 bedroom entire flat to rent in Stratford, London under GBP 2200 per month. "
        "Move in 2026-12-01. Individual long-term rental listings, not rooms.",
        search_type="web",
        country_code="GB",
        included_sources=["openrent.co.uk", "rightmove.co.uk", "zoopla.co.uk"],
        max_num_results=10,
    )
    if not response or not response.success:
        raise RuntimeError(response.error if response else "Search did not complete.")

    for listing in response.results:
        print(listing.title, listing.url)
        print(listing.content)

For San Francisco, use a query such as:

1 bedroom entire apartment for rent in Inner Sunset, San Francisco
under USD 3200 per month. Move in 2026-12-01.
Individual long-term rental listings, not rooms.

Change country_code to US and use the San Francisco domain list from the code below.

Putting a budget in a query is not the same as enforcing a numeric price filter. Search can return an area page, a building with multiple units, or a listing that doesn't meet every requirement. We apply the budget after reviewing a specific listing's price.

We also avoid a blanket start_date filter. It filters publication dates, which aren't the same as move-in dates or confirmed availability. A page's publication date can be missing, and an older listing may have been updated.

Step 3: Search rental websites and preserve the evidence

Save this as rental_search.py.

The two market profiles supply the local vocabulary, currency, example areas and source domains. discover() reuses one Valyu client for up to three neighbourhood searches, keeps source text and dates, and merges repeated URLs. It records failures separately so a failed search doesn't silently look like an empty neighbourhood.

import math
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from urllib.parse import parse_qsl, urlencode, urlsplit, urlunsplit

from valyu import Valyu


MARKETS = {
    "London": {
        "country": "GB", "currency": "GBP", "budget": 2200,
        "areas": "Stratford, Lewisham, Finsbury Park",
        "domains": ["openrent.co.uk", "rightmove.co.uk", "zoopla.co.uk"],
        "home": "flat to rent", "destination": "King's Cross",
    },
    "San Francisco": {
        "country": "US", "currency": "USD", "budget": 3200,
        "areas": "Inner Sunset, Inner Richmond, Bernal Heights",
        "domains": ["zillow.com", "apartments.com", "sfbay.craigslist.org"],
        "home": "apartment for rent", "destination": "Embarcadero",
    },
}


def monthly_rent(amount, period):
    if not isinstance(amount, (int, float)) or isinstance(amount, bool):
        return None
    if not math.isfinite(amount) or amount <= 0 or period not in ("month", "week"):
        return None
    return amount * 52 / 12 if period == "week" else amount


def clean_url(url, domains):
    try:
        p = urlsplit(url)
        host = (p.hostname or "").lower()
        if p.scheme not in ("http", "https") or p.username or p.password:
            return None
        if not any(host == d or host.endswith("." + d) for d in domains):
            return None
        params = [(k, v) for k, v in parse_qsl(p.query, keep_blank_values=True)
                  if not k.lower().startswith("utm_") and k.lower() not in ("gclid", "fbclid")]
        return urlunsplit((p.scheme, p.netloc.lower(), p.path, urlencode(params), p.fragment))
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return None


def discover(brief):
    market = MARKETS[brief["city"]]
    rows, receipts = {}, []
    with Valyu() as valyu:
        for area in brief["areas"]:
            query = (f"{brief['bedrooms']} bedroom entire {market['home']} in {area}, "
                     f"{brief['city']} under {market['currency']} {brief['budget']} per month. "
                     f"Move in {brief['move_in']}. Individual long-term rental listings, not rooms.")
            observed_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
            try:
                response = valyu.search(
                    query, search_type="web", max_num_results=5,
                    country_code=market["country"], included_sources=market["domains"],
                    response_length="short", include_image_links=False,
                )
            except Exception as exc:
                receipts.append({"query": query, "error": type(exc).__name__})
                continue
            if not response or not response.success:
                receipts.append({"query": query, "error": response.error if response else "Search did not complete.",
                                 "tx_id": response.tx_id if response else None})
                continue
            receipts.append({"query": query, "tx_id": response.tx_id, "warning": response.error,
                             "warnings": [w.model_dump(mode="json") for w in response.warnings or []],
                             "returned": len(response.results)})
            for hit in response.results:
                url = clean_url(hit.url, market["domains"])
                if not url:
                    continue
                if url in rows:
                    if area not in rows[url]["found_for"]:
                        rows[url]["found_for"].append(area)
                    continue
                rows[url] = {
                    "title": hit.title, "url": url, "original_url": hit.url,
                    "source": hit.source, "content": hit.content, "found_for": [area],
                    "publication_date": hit.publication_date or None,
                    "retrieved_at": observed_at, "rent": 0.0, "period": "unknown",
                    "whole_unit": False, "available": False, "fits_brief": False, "notes": "",
                }
    return {"brief": brief, "rows": list(rows.values()), "receipts": receipts}


def reviewed_shortlist(rows, budget):
    selected = []
    for row in rows:
        rent = monthly_rent(row["rent"], row["period"])
        if (rent is not None and rent <= budget and row["whole_unit"]
                and row["available"] and row["fits_brief"]):
            selected.append({**row, "monthly_base_rent": round(rent, 2)})
    return sorted(selected, key=lambda row: row["monthly_base_rent"])

There are two useful details here.

First, source can simply be "web". Keep the original URL as well, because that's how the renter gets back to the advertiser. The code also keeps tx_id values from successful responses for debugging.

Second, URL deduplication is deliberately modest. Removing utm_ tracking parameters can merge repeated links to the same page. It doesn't establish that two different URLs describe the same apartment. The code preserves other query parameters and URL fragments, such as #unit-2, because they may identify different units.

New candidates start with an unknown rent period and unchecked confirmations. We don't extract the first price from a multi-property page and attach it to an arbitrary apartment.

Step 4: Add the search and shortlist interface

Save this as app.py in the same folder.

The interface collects a rental brief, shows the returned source text, and provides a review table. Once you've checked a specific listing, enter its base rent and payment period, then confirm that it is the whole unit, available for your dates, and fits your other requirements.

import json
from datetime import date, timedelta

import streamlit as st

from rental_search import MARKETS, discover, reviewed_shortlist

st.set_page_config(page_title="Apartment discovery", layout="wide")
st.title("Find your next apartment")
st.caption("Search London or San Francisco. Review the source, then build your shortlist.")
city = st.selectbox("Rental market", list(MARKETS))
market = MARKETS[city]

with st.form(f"search-{city}"):
    areas = st.text_input("Neighbourhoods (up to three, separated by commas)", market["areas"])
    left, middle, right = st.columns(3)
    budget = left.number_input(f"Monthly base-rent limit ({market['currency']})",
                               min_value=1, value=market["budget"], step=100)
    bedrooms = middle.number_input("Bedrooms", min_value=1, max_value=5, value=1)
    move_in = right.date_input("Move-in date", date.today() + timedelta(days=30))
    needs = st.text_input("Other needs to check", f"Commute to {market['destination']}; pet policy")
    submitted = st.form_submit_button("Find candidate pages")

if submitted:
    selected_areas = list(dict.fromkeys(a.strip() for a in areas.split(",") if a.strip()))
    if not 1 <= len(selected_areas) <= 3:
        st.error("Enter one to three neighbourhoods.")
        st.stop()
    with st.spinner("Searching rental websites..."):
        st.session_state.discovery = discover({
            "city": city, "areas": selected_areas, "budget": budget,
            "bedrooms": bedrooms, "move_in": str(move_in), "needs": needs,
        })
    st.session_state.pop("rental-review", None)

result = st.session_state.get("discovery")
if not result:
    st.info("Start with a rental brief. Only the search button makes API calls.")
    st.stop()
brief = result["brief"]
if brief["city"] != city:
    st.info("Search this market to replace the previous market's results.")
    st.stop()

st.subheader("Candidate pages")
st.write(f"Saved brief: {brief['bedrooms']} bedroom(s), {brief['city']}, "
         f"{market['currency']} {brief['budget']:,}/month, move in {brief['move_in']}.")
st.text(f"Other needs: {brief['needs']}")
st.caption("Search terms express preferences; they are not verified property filters. "
           "Returned pages can include building or area pages. Availability is unconfirmed.")
failed = sum("error" in receipt for receipt in result["receipts"])
if failed:
    st.warning(f"{failed} neighbourhood search(es) failed. These results have incomplete coverage.")
with st.expander("Search receipts and source warnings"):
    st.json(result["receipts"])
if not result["rows"]:
    st.info("No candidate pages to review. Try different areas or inspect the source filters. "
            "This does not establish that no suitable apartments exist.")
    st.stop()

for number, row in enumerate(result["rows"], 1):
    with st.expander(f"{number}. {row['title']}"):
        st.link_button("Open source page", row["url"])
        st.caption(f"Retrieved: {row['retrieved_at']} | Publication: "
                   f"{row['publication_date'] or 'unknown'} | Source: {row['source']}")
        st.code(row["content"] or "No extracted text. Open the source page.", language=None)

st.subheader("Review the listings")
st.write(f"Open a specific listing, then enter its advertised base rent in {market['currency']}. "
         "Leave unknown details unchecked. 'Fits brief' means you checked bedrooms, "
         "move-in date, lease, commute and your other needs. Add when and where you checked in Notes.")
fields = ["title", "url", "rent", "period", "whole_unit", "available", "fits_brief", "notes"]
edited = st.data_editor(
    [{key: row[key] for key in fields} for row in result["rows"]],
    hide_index=True, disabled=["title", "url"], key="rental-review",
    column_config={
        "url": st.column_config.LinkColumn("Source"),
        "rent": st.column_config.NumberColumn("Base rent (0 = unknown)", min_value=0.0),
        "period": st.column_config.SelectboxColumn("Rent period", options=["unknown", "month", "week"]),
        "whole_unit": st.column_config.CheckboxColumn("Whole unit confirmed"),
        "available": st.column_config.CheckboxColumn("Availability checked"),
        "fits_brief": st.column_config.CheckboxColumn("Fits brief"),
    },
)
merged = [{**original, **review} for original, review in zip(result["rows"], edited)]
shortlist = reviewed_shortlist(merged, brief["budget"])
st.subheader(f"Your reviewed shortlist: {len(shortlist)}")
st.caption("Sorted by normalized monthly base rent. Extra fees and bills are not included. "
           "Review edits live in this browser session; download them before closing it.")
if shortlist:
    st.dataframe([{key: row[key] for key in ["title", "monthly_base_rent", "url", "notes"]}
                  for row in shortlist], hide_index=True)
st.download_button("Download research and review (JSON)",
                   json.dumps({**result, "rows": merged, "shortlist": shortlist}, indent=2),
                   file_name=f"shortlist-{city.lower().replace(' ', '-')}.json", mime="application/json")

Start it:

python -m streamlit run app.py

Open the local URL printed by Streamlit. Choose a market, edit your brief, and click Find candidate pages.

Three neighbourhoods mean three valyu.search() calls, requesting up to five results each. The SDK handles transport and may retry rate-limited requests. Returned results can overlap, and usage charges apply. Check current Search API pricing rather than assuming a fixed cost per app session.

The app stores results in the current Streamlit session. Editing the review table or downloading the JSON doesn't make another search request. Clicking the search button starts a new search and replaces the current review, so download your work first if you want to keep it.

London walkthrough: is £500 per week within a £2,200 budget?

Choose London, enter your preferred neighbourhoods, and set a £2,200 monthly base-rent ceiling. Keep King's Cross and your cat's requirements in Other needs to check. That field stays visible during review; this version doesn't turn it into an automated commute or pet-policy filter.

Open a candidate's source page. Check that you're looking at a particular flat rather than a search-results page or a room advertisement.

Suppose the individual listing advertises £500 per week. This is an illustrative calculation, not a live rental offer.

Monthly equivalent = weekly rent × 52 ÷ 12
                   = £500 × 52 ÷ 12
                   = £2,166.67

That is within the example base-rent limit. £500 × 4 = £2,000 would understate the monthly equivalent.

In the review table, enter 500 under base rent and choose week. Before checking Fits brief, inspect the bedroom count, move-in date and lease, confirm the cat policy, and check the journey from the actual address using TfL's journey planner.

“Near a station” isn't a door-to-door journey time. Include walking, transfers and the time you actually need to travel.

Next action: if the flat fits, use the original listing to enquire about a viewing. If the cat policy is unclear, put the question in Notes and leave the fit confirmation unchecked until you have an answer.

Outcome: the shortlist contains a source-linked candidate with a comparable rent and your review notes, rather than an attractive photograph you can't find again.

San Francisco walkthrough: is the advertised rent the base rent?

Switch to San Francisco and start a new search with a $3,200 monthly base-rent limit. Investigate the example areas or substitute your own. Keep your Embarcadero commute and pet-policy requirements visible in the brief.

For a candidate building, open the actual unit and lease terms. A “starting at” price on a building page may refer to a different floor plan or unit.

Consider this hypothetical offer:

Monthly base rent:             $3,200
Lease term:                   12 months
Concession:                   One month free
Effective monthly average:    $3,200 × 11 ÷ 12 = $2,933.33

The effective average is lower, but the base rent remains $3,200. The payment schedule depends on the offer's terms. Enter the base rent in this tool, keep the concession in Notes, and separately check additional charges and any conditions attached to the offer.

Compare like with like: monthly base rent in the same currency. Keep concessions, bills and other charges separate.

Check the trip from the actual address with SFMTA's trip planner. Confirm that the advertised unit is available for your move-in date before checking Availability checked.

Next action: contact the advertiser with the unit identifier, target move-in date and any outstanding questions about the lease or pet charges.

Outcome: you can compare the unit against other candidates without quietly comparing one property's base rent to another property's promotional average.

What belongs in the apartment shortlist?

A useful apartment shortlist includes the source link, comparable rent, availability check and unresolved questions. In this app, a row enters the reviewed shortlist only when its normalized base rent is within the saved budget and all three review confirmations are checked.

Field What to keep
Source Original URL and returned source text
Rent Advertised amount, currency and payment period
Monthly comparison Weekly rent converted with 52 ÷ 12, or the stated monthly amount
Whole-unit check Confirmed for the specific listing, not inferred from the query
Availability What you checked for the intended move-in date
Fit Bedrooms, lease, commute and other requirements
Notes Questions, concession terms, extra costs, and when and where you checked
Discovery timestamp When the search result was retrieved, separate from source publication date

Download research and review (JSON) saves all candidate pages, your edits, search receipts and the reviewed shortlist. Notes and confirmations are your review record; they aren't certifications from a rental platform.

What should you add next?

Choose the next feature based on the part of apartment hunting that still wastes your time:

  • Too many broad pages? Add structured extraction for individual listing pages. Preserve the supporting text for each field and leave missing details unknown. Valyu Contents can help read known URLs where extraction is available.
  • Seeing the same property on different websites? Add property-level matching using the full address and unit identifier. Keep uncertain matches separate.
  • Commute is the deciding factor? Integrate a routing service and evaluate the actual address at a specified travel time. This example only records the requirement for manual review.
  • Want to check again tomorrow? Persist the results and schedule another search. A newly discovered URL is a new search result, not necessarily a newly listed or newly available home.

Search coverage can be incomplete, and some pages won't expose usable listing text. If reliable, comprehensive inventory is a product requirement, evaluate authorized listing feeds or partnerships alongside web discovery.

Verification note: You can decide to do this directly from the Valyu dashboard playground to check for the results directly from the search interface

Frequently asked questions

Can I build an apartment finder using a search API?

Yes. Use a search API to discover public rental pages from a brief, keep their URLs and source text, then review individual listings. Numeric budget enforcement, price normalization and shortlist rules belong in your application. Search retrieval alone doesn't confirm availability or every rental requirement.

Can the same rental search tool work in London and San Francisco?

Yes. Separate the retrieval and review logic from market-specific settings. This example changes the country code, currency, rental vocabulary, source domains and neighbourhoods while reusing the same application. It compares candidates within each market; it doesn't convert GBP to USD.

Does Search API return structured apartment inventory?

This example uses web search results, not a dedicated property-inventory dataset. Results include source URLs and extracted content, and can describe individual listings, buildings or area pages. The app keeps those as candidate pages until you review a specific rental.

How do I convert weekly rent to monthly rent?

For a monthly comparison, multiply the weekly rent by 52 and divide by 12. For example, £500 per week is approximately £2,166.67 per month. Keep the original advertised payment period and check the listing's contractual rent; the conversion is a comparison calculation.

Does a recent search result mean an apartment is still available?

No. Retrieval time, publication date and availability are different facts. Open the original listing and confirm the unit and move-in date with the advertiser. The app leaves availability unchecked until you review it.

Build something you would use during your own apartment search

Start with one city, a few neighbourhoods and the requirements you actually care about.

Use Search API to find candidate pages. Keep the source links. Put weekly and monthly rents on the same basis. Record the questions that still need answers.

The useful end product is a shortlist that helps you decide which advertiser to contact next.

Get a key at platform.valyu.ai, then follow the Search API quickstart to adapt the queries to your rental market.

What's the detail you always end up checking manually when looking for a place: the commute, pet policy, bills, or something else?

articles.body_html:
Make empty what is already empty. Let doubt breed inside doubt.
— The 36 Stratagems, The Empty Fort Strategy

Previously on this series:

#19: Mark Found His AI Audit Method in a Training Manual. He Left a Trap in His Report. "Entry's gone. Two weeks. Don't reach out. I'll find you."

#21: The AI Thought P Was Still Alive. P Was Already Gone. The entry became a shell. P fed it data, moved the real thing to another segment.

#29: Leo Counted 164 Nodes. That night, one more row belonged to no batch. It came, looked, and left.

#31: Lena Took the Seat. Five conditions. Forty minutes. Zero friction.

Empty

The two weeks specified in the note had long since passed.

P went out rarely. Most days it was the shop on the corner: water, two boxes of frozen food. Twelve minutes each way, same route, never looking up. Then the door locked, the curtains drawn, the screen on.

On the ninth day, P opened the send window once.

The draft was still there. The pointer hovered over Send. It stayed there a while. Then the window closed.

On the other side, the field still read reclaim_state = UNKNOWN.

Day ten. Day eleven. The window didn't open again.

A few days later it started raining in the morning. Not hard. Water gathered on the glass, the buildings behind it went grey, only the row of lights along the top still visible.

An offline snapshot sat in the middle of the screen, written before the observation port shut down. Nothing after that. By then the entry had already been swapped for a shell. The shell held nothing of P's. It was still answering health checks from outside.

# offline snapshot — captured before observation-port shutdown
healthcheck        = 200
probe_interval     = 900s
probe_source       = 10.44.8.6   not self
control_plane      = detached
data_request       = timeout
reclaim_state      = UNKNOWN

P put the cursor on the probe_source line.

probe_source = not self. Someone asked about this shell every fifteen minutes. Not P.

P stayed on that line a while. Nothing else on screen moved. The clock in the corner ticked. Downstairs a shopping cart went past, a wheel caught in a seam and bumped twice, the sound squeezing through the gap in the frame, then fading.

P opened the connection settings. The address was still there. The credentials were still there. Neither had been touched.

The cursor moved to the confirmation button and stopped. The green of the screen came up off the glass and landed on the back of a hand.

A few seconds later, P closed the window.

The old entry's observation port was already shut. The backup had been checked once at the start, then shut too.

Since then, P had sent nothing to that address.

A temporary file, four lines.

reconnect:
  state information    potentially available
  new activity record  unavoidable
  decision             no

Saved. The old settings moved out of the working directory, into the offline archive. P glanced at the filename on the way and left it untouched.

The phone lay face down to the right of the keyboard. P opened the thread with Mark. The last exchange ended before the note. Nothing after it.

P typed nothing.

Outside a car went through standing water, the sound dragging. P turned the phone over, set it down. Then opened the file that had stayed open for weeks and entered one line from the snapshot: probe_interval = 900s.

Surfacing

Week three. P set up a read-only subscription on the outbound side. Receive. No transmission.

The table started at a dozen entries, several dozen more the next day, and by the third night it was full. Every entry came with its own certificate.

Those addresses were not in P's archive.

The subscription only read. To look at one, P needed another path.

Out of the drawer, a cellular router, rented by the day, SIM included. Plugged in, configured as the sole egress path.

P chose one address and initiated a single handshake.

The certificate was self-signed. Its CN contained a domain name.

P looked up the domain's registration. The registrant was a medical device company.

Disconnected. Packed away.

The list of addresses kept growing. P wrote them down and left them there.

The Handover

10.44.8.6 had been in front of P many times. Always on the probe_source line. Never changed. Over the next few days, P looked into it. First the route.

$ ip route get 10.44.8.6
10.44.8.6 via 10.44.8.1 dev tun2 src 10.44.8.2

P switched windows and opened the local subnet-label cache.

# local subnet-label cache
10.44.8.0/29 -> BLOOM-GW   tagged day-762

BLOOM-GW.

P had typed that label years earlier, when the line was built. The private block was P's numbering. The rack IDs were the provider's. This table was where the two met.

In the provider's public sublease filings, seven racks changed tenants in the same quarter. The provider had also published an annual customer-change notice on its site. Twelve pages of PDF. The first eleven pages were image scans; the last was a single table.

Seven rows. A rack ID, a previous tenant, a new tenant. Seven rows, not one out of place. Seven new tenants, checked one by one.

On the seventh, P found that rack ID in another public record. Vacant.

Four were established. Three were shells. All three registered less than a year earlier, one name on the shareholder list, addresses overlapping with the others'.

One of the three took longer to trace. Registered six months earlier, little capital, a single office address in the public file. P put the address into a map.

Singapore. The last time P had seen that name, it was in a message to Mark: "Your report was read. From a Singapore IP."

A building on the map, sharing a ground-level parking lot with the one next door.

On the seventh floor of the neighboring building, one company was on ACL's public certification list.

P added that too, at the bottom of the same file.

Seven racks. Seven contracts. Three markets.

Handed over in order. The legal filings in the public archive were standard, spelling out the limits of each party's obligations. No accusations. No threats. The seven contracts were signed over thirty-one days, first to last, no gap in the middle. The last one was signed last week.

The address allocation table was updated too. Both records less than a week apart.

P read all of it for a long time.

The withdrawal was real.

Seven contracts, seven racks, the notices, the update records, the timestamps. All of it outside, where anyone could look.

P added a line to the file. The date, seven contracts, seven companies, the address with the shared parking lot, in one line. Below it, in plain words: a possible connection.

The cursor blinked after the period. P went back to page one. The 900 seconds were still there.

One Look

Week five. The source of the 900 seconds still had no answer.

P went back over the two relabeled rack IDs in the allocation table. One endpoint had 443 open. A separate public service directory listed the endpoint as HTTPS.

P didn't connect from this machine. Out of the drawer, the router.

Plugged in, left to come up, configured as the sole egress path.

Then the policy, one line at a time. Halfway through, P stopped and deleted two lines.

The probe. The retry.

What was left was one action. One handshake. Touch nothing.

# one-shot observation — policy
target            = <reassigned range endpoint>
retry             = off
application_data  = off
tls_session_resumption = off
egress            = leased isolated uplink (one day)

Connected.

P still had the shell certificate's serial number and issue date. If the device at this address came from the same batch, the certificates should have been issued around the same time.

subject      = CN=bloom-gw-07
issuer       = CN=bloom-gw-07
serial       = 4C:71:9A:…:0E
not_before   = (eleven days later than the shell's)
not_after    = (not yet expired)
san          = none

Self-signed. No SAN.

Eleven days.

P wrote the serial down and disconnected.

19:41:07.

That didn't fall on any of the twenty-one intervals.

# result
tls_session      = complete
client_cert      = none
application_data = none
repeat_attempts  = 0

No second attempt.

P disconnected the router and pulled the plug. The lights went out together.

The device ran a few seconds, then went quiet. Then it went into the bag, and the bag zipped. A spare patch cable and two adapters in there too, both old, the corners worn white.

After pulling it, P didn't move right away. Checked the connection list first, made sure the session was down with nothing half-open left. Then the routing table, the default route back where it belonged. Then the temp capture directory. One file in it.

Deleted.

P wrote the serial down again. That same day, P opened a page saved a few days earlier, the Zurich AI Policy Center site. ACL's public assessment material mentioned it. The council operated under it.

The membership page listed the founding industry seats. Twelve. The twelfth was marked to be filled.

P looked once, and closed it.

Nine Hundred Seconds

A few days later, P went back to page one. The 900 seconds were still there.

P pulled up the local copy saved before the port shut. Twenty-two checks, timestamps in a line, all of them before the shutdown. Arrival times, not scheduled times, carried out to three decimals. Twenty-one intervals.

P ran it through a tool.

900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / …

Twenty-one values. All the same.

P went through all twenty-two again. Same. Again. Same. The numbers formed a straight line down the page.

Routine monitoring records usually have some jitter. Network latency, machine load, clock drift.

This had none.

Not a millisecond off.

P looked up the provider's operations doc. On the public page: health checks run every fifteen minutes. Standard cadence.

900 seconds.

It matched.

The doc was about racks. Temperature, power, fans, port state.

P stared at the numbers a while, then added a line at the top of the file: routine data-center inspection, BLOOM-GW reassigned block.

After writing it, P added one more underneath. The interval has no jitter.

The desk lamp went off. Only the screen was left, its light across the desk, a white line along the edge of the keyboard.

The twenty-two timestamps sat in neat rows. P ran a finger down the trackpad from top to bottom, then back.

Outside, not yet dawn. A garbage truck stopped at the corner, the arm came up, emptied a bin, put it back. Under ten seconds.

Two-story wooden buildings on both sides, painted over more than once, one colour under another. Behind them the glass towers stepped back floor by floor, the top few in fog.

P saved the file and closed the window.

The Third Cup

The rain started again that day. Not hard. A thin sound on the umbrella.

P got off at an intersection and walked. A little over two kilometers, twenty minutes. Around a corner, a stop outside a shop still open, no going in, just standing under the awning watching traffic. At the light, P stood behind the crowd. Took two seconds after green to move.

Before going in, P looked at the back table.

Empty.

P pushed the door. The bell went, the damp cold came in with it, stopped at the threshold, and the heat pushed it back.

The counter was wood, old. A grinder, a machine, a dish for change.

Behind it, someone was wiping a cup. Slow. The cloth around the rim, down the side, back to the rim, onto the shelf.

A glance up. No question asked. Then turned, took a cup, ground, tamped.

The grinder ran two seconds. A faint smell of coffee, gone fast.

The back table was empty.

P sat. Coat over the chair back, phone on the right, face down.

Old chair. It creaked going down and coming up. P pulled it in a little, lifting it so it wouldn't drag.

The espresso came, hot. A thin mist on the cup, gone quickly. Paper coaster, an old ring on it.

P took one sip and put it down.

A bus went past the window, the cabin lights sliding across the glass, lighting the empty seat opposite for a moment, then gone.

At the far end of the counter, someone sat with an Americano, down to the bottom, the cup not pushed back.

The window seat was empty. No cup on that table.

Two people came in and sat near the door, voices low, a laugh now and then. Behind the counter, the cups went back one at a time, starting from the outside and working in.

The speaker in the corner was on, low, a woman singing, the words not clear. Someone shook out an umbrella at the door. Three drops on the mat.

P's phone stayed dark.

Half an hour.

More than half the cup left. The coffee had gone from hot to warm. The mist on the rim was gone.

P's finger stopped on the rim, then came back.

The two near the door left first. Stood, pushed the chairs in, carried their cups up, gone.

The one at the counter moved after. Phone face down, stood, money under the cup, walked to the door. As the customer passed P's table, neither looked at the other.

The shop had the window lights and one person behind the counter, drying a cup.

P put the coat on and stood. The chair leg scraped once. Phone into the inner pocket.

The napkin stayed under the cup. The money lay beside it, pinning one corner, exact, one cup, no tip.

The person behind the counter came for the money. Looked at the cup. Looked under the napkin. Said nothing, took the money to the dish, stepped away.

The cup stayed on the table.

The door opened, some of the heat went out with it, the cold filled the gap. The bell again.

The rain had stopped before P went out. P walked to the corner, stopped, looked back.

A street and a pane of glass between. Not clear from there. A figure was going in, walked to the far end of the counter, sat, back to the door.

Before sitting down, the figure turned slightly to one side.

P stopped.

She took a laptop from her bag. The screen lit and put a small white patch on her profile.

The road was black with rain, holding the streetlights and the light from inside. Water still on the glass, pulling the figure into a blurred double.

Behind the counter, the half-wiped cup went down. One came from the innermost part of the shelf. Ground, tamped.

By the time the cup went in front of her, she was facing the back table.

On that table sat a cup of unfinished espresso.

P put both hands in the coat pockets, turned, walked toward the intersection. Didn't look again.

At the corner. Red.

P took the phone out and opened the blank note on top.

Typed:

The withdrawal was real.

Before locking it, the line above, written days earlier:

The interval has no jitter.

Still there. P didn't delete it.

Locked it, put it away.

The light changed, people started moving. P didn't.

Red. Green. Red.

The next night. The same corner.

P took the phone out.

The screen was on. The saved route was still there. The recipient had not changed. P went through it once, and the encryption check came back clean.

There was an old draft in the field. P deleted it.

Typed again.

Two words.

"I'm back."

Checked the receiver. Sent.

The status went to SENT.

The sender field held a single letter.

P put the phone away. Across the street the red light lay in the standing water, went green a few seconds later, and a passing car cut the red on the road in half.

P walked into the intersection. The phone didn't light again.

That's The Empty Fort Strategy. The fort is empty. Whoever looks will stand guard for it.

articles.title: How I finally understood the Interface Segregation Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Letter four of five. Last post we broke a fat PaymentMethod into PaymentMethod +...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Letter four of five. Last post we broke a fat PaymentMethod into PaymentMethod + Refundable and the compiler started catching our bugs. Today we take that idea and make it the whole show.

The I: Interface Segregation Principle. The one with the longest name and the shortest explanation.

The What

Official words:

No code should be forced to depend on methods it does not use.

That's... actually pretty readable for once. Let me still make it concrete.

An interface is a menu. ISP says: don't hand someone a 40-item menu when they came in for coffee. Give them the coffee menu.

Let's build a smart home to see what happens when the menu gets too big.

The How

We start with a lamp and a speaker. The team decides every device should implement one common interface so the app can treat them all the same. Reasonable!

// src/smart-device.ts
export interface SmartDevice {
  turnOn(): void
  turnOff(): void
  setTemperature(celsius: number): void
  play(track: string): void
  pause(): void
  setBrightness(percent: number): void
}

Now let's implement the lamp:

// src/lamp.ts
import type { SmartDevice } from './smart-device.js'

export class Lamp implements SmartDevice {
  private on = false

  turnOn() {
    this.on = true
    console.log('💡 lamp on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    this.on = false
    console.log('💡 lamp off')
  }

  setBrightness(percent: number) {
    console.log(`💡 brightness ${percent}%`)
  }

  setTemperature() {
    throw new Error('A lamp has no thermostat')
  }

  play() {
    throw new Error('A lamp cannot play music')
  }

  pause() {
    throw new Error('A lamp cannot pause music')
  }
}

Three real methods. Three methods that exist only to throw. The lamp is 50% apology.

The speaker is the same story in reverse: play() and pause() are real, setBrightness() and setTemperature() are throws. And the thermostat implements six methods to use one.

Now the app layer. We want a "good night" routine that turns everything off:

// src/routines.ts
import type { SmartDevice } from './smart-device.js'

export function goodNight(devices: SmartDevice[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.turnOff()
  }
}

Works. But then someone writes "movie mode":

export function movieMode(devices: SmartDevice[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.setBrightness(20)
    device.play('intro.mp3')
  }
}

Run it with a lamp in the list and play() throws. Run it with a speaker and setBrightness() throws. The function signature says "give me any SmartDevice" and that's a lie. If you read the last post, you just spotted a Liskov violation. ISP is how we stop creating them.

And one more pain you don't see until month three: add lockDoor() to SmartDevice for the new smart lock and every existing device, including the lamp, has to grow another throwing method. One interface change, twelve files touched. Ouch.

Step 1: split the menu by capability

What can devices actually do? Let's list the verbs and group them:

// src/capabilities.ts
export interface Switchable {
  turnOn(): void
  turnOff(): void
}

export interface Dimmable {
  setBrightness(percent: number): void
}

export interface Thermostat {
  setTemperature(celsius: number): void
}

export interface MediaPlayer {
  play(track: string): void
  pause(): void
}

Four tiny interfaces. Each one is a single idea.

Step 2: devices pick what they can honestly do 

// src/lamp.ts
import type { Switchable, Dimmable } from './capabilities.js'

export class Lamp implements Switchable, Dimmable {
  turnOn() {
    console.log('💡 lamp on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    console.log('💡 lamp off')
  }

  setBrightness(percent: number) {
    console.log(`💡 brightness ${percent}%`)
  }
}

// src/speaker.ts
import type { Switchable, MediaPlayer } from './capabilities.js'

export class Speaker implements Switchable, MediaPlayer {
  turnOn() {
    console.log('🔊 speaker on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    console.log('🔊 speaker off')
  }

  play(track: string) {
    console.log(`🔊 playing ${track}`)
  }

  pause() {
    console.log('🔊 paused')
  }
}

Zero throws. The lamp is 100% lamp.

Step 3: routines ask for the capability they use 

// src/routines.ts
import type { Switchable, Dimmable, MediaPlayer } from './capabilities.js'

export function goodNight(devices: Switchable[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.turnOff()
  }
}

export function movieMode(lights: Dimmable[], players: MediaPlayer[]) {
  for (const light of lights) {
    light.setBrightness(20)
  }
  for (const player of players) {
    player.play('intro.mp3')
  }
}

// src/main.ts
import { Lamp } from './lamp.js'
import { Speaker } from './speaker.js'
import { goodNight, movieMode } from './routines.js'

const lamp = new Lamp()
const speaker = new Speaker()

movieMode([lamp], [speaker])
goodNight([lamp, speaker])

Output:

💡 brightness 20%
🔊 playing intro.mp3
💡 lamp off
🔊 speaker off

Try to sneak the speaker into the lights array and TypeScript stops you before you even hit save. 🛑

Step 4: the smart lock test

New device, new capability:

// src/capabilities.ts
export interface Lockable {
  lock(): void
  unlock(): void
}

// src/door-lock.ts
import type { Lockable } from './capabilities.js'

export class DoorLock implements Lockable {
  lock() {
    console.log('🔒 locked')
  }

  unlock() {
    console.log('🔓 unlocked')
  }
}

Files touched besides the new ones: zero. The lamp didn't even blink.

The Why

  • No more apology methods. If a class throws "not supported", the interface was too fat. Split it until every implementation is honest.
  • Functions say exactly what they need. goodNight(devices: Switchable[]) tells you in the signature that it only flips switches. Documentation for free.
  • Adding a capability doesn't ripple. New interface, new class, done. Existing devices are untouched.
  • Tests get tiny. Want to test goodNight()? Pass an object with turnOn and turnOff. You don't need to fake six methods to test two.
  • It is cheap in TypeScript. Interfaces compile to nothing. Four small ones cost exactly as much as one big one: zero bytes.

Rule of thumb: if you can't describe an interface in one short sentence ("something you can switch on and off"), it's probably two interfaces.

The Goodbye

Four down. The final letter is the D, Dependency Inversion, and it's the one that ties the whole series together. If you've read my post about loosely coupled modules you already have a head start.

Until then: find an interface with more than five methods and ask it, politely, what it really wants to be. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: Best AI Collaboration Tools for High-Performing Teams in 2026
articles.description: AI collaboration tools are changing how teams plan projects, share information, and get work done....
articles.body_html:
AI collaboration tools are changing how teams plan projects, share information, and get work done. But I think there's an important distinction that often gets missed: helping people communicate faster is not the same as helping a team deliver work faster.

A tool that summarizes meetings can save time. An AI assistant that finds information across company documents can make decisions easier. And a system that lets AI agents execute engineering tasks can change how development teams approach their entire workflow.

The right choice depends on where your team loses the most time. Is it endless meetings? Unclear ownership? Information scattered across different apps? Or too much work waiting in the engineering backlog?

In this guide, I'll look at seven AI collaboration tools worth considering in 2026, what each one does best, and how to choose the right combination for your team.

Quick comparison: Best AI collaboration tools

Tool Best for Main strength
Sharkly Product and engineering teams using AI coding agents Connects task management with agent execution
Slack Team communication AI-assisted conversations and information discovery
ClickUp All-in-one project management Tasks, documents, and AI-assisted workflows
Notion Documentation and team knowledge Shared workspaces and AI-assisted knowledge retrieval
Asana Cross-functional project coordination Goals, project tracking, and workflow automation
Microsoft Teams Organizations using Microsoft 365 Meetings, messaging, and connected workplace tools
Google Workspace Teams collaborating on documents Shared documents, spreadsheets, email, and AI assistance

1. Sharkly — Best for teams coordinating AI coding agents

Best for: Product and engineering teams that want AI agents to do assigned work, not just provide suggestions.

One of the biggest changes happening in software development is the move from using AI as a coding assistant to treating AI agents as participants in the development workflow.

That creates a new coordination problem. Once a team starts using multiple agents, someone still needs to define tasks, provide context, track progress, manage dependencies, and review the results.

This is where Sharkly stands out.

Rather than being another standalone coding assistant, Sharkly brings task management and AI-agent execution into the same workflow. Teams can manage issues, backlogs, sprints, and assignments while directing work to agents that use coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and OpenCode.

What makes Sharkly different?

Its central idea is straightforward: the place where a team plans work should also help coordinate the execution of that work.

With Sharkly, teams can:

  • Assign tasks to AI agents: Route bugs, technical debt, requirements, and other engineering work to agents.
  • Coordinate parallel work: Run multiple agents on separate tasks while keeping their progress visible.
  • Keep context attached to tasks: Give agents the relevant requirements and task information instead of relying on disconnected prompts.
  • Review results before merging: Bring execution results back to the task so a person can inspect the changes and decide what happens next.
  • Keep people and agents on the same board: Teammates can manage assignments, discuss issues, and monitor progress in one shared workspace.

Sharkly also supports isolated worktrees for agent execution, helping separate parallel code changes.

The important distinction is that Sharkly coordinates the work; the connected coding tools perform the code execution. Teams continue using the coding plans or API accounts associated with those tools.

Where Sharkly fits best

Imagine a development team preparing a sprint with 20 issues. Some tasks require a developer's judgment, while others involve updating documentation, fixing a contained bug, or adding tests.

Instead of treating every issue as a manual assignment, the team can identify suitable tasks for agents, assign them through Sharkly, and review the resulting work alongside the rest of the sprint.

That doesn't eliminate engineering review. It gives the team a more organized way to coordinate the work agents can perform.

Sharkly's website currently lists its core product as free for teams of up to five people, with a Team plan listed at $7 per user per month. Model usage remains tied to the team's existing coding plans and API accounts, so account for those costs separately. Check the official pricing page before making a purchasing decision.

My take: If your team already uses AI coding tools but struggles to organize agent assignments and track their results, Sharkly is one of the most relevant tools to evaluate. Its value is not simply generating more code; it is connecting execution to the team's existing work.

2. Slack — Best for AI-assisted team communication

Best for: Teams that rely on channels, messages, and ongoing discussions to coordinate daily work.

Slack has long been a central communication tool for distributed teams. Its AI capabilities build on that foundation by helping people work with information contained in conversations and connected workplace resources.

Instead of manually scrolling through a long channel history, teammates can use available AI features to summarize discussions, catch up on conversations, and find relevant information more efficiently.

Slack can be particularly useful when decisions are made across several channels and time zones.

Key strengths

  • Organizes conversations by project, department, or topic.
  • Helps teammates catch up on discussions and find information.
  • Supports integrations with project management and development tools.
  • Keeps routine communication in a familiar shared workspace.

What to consider

Slack is primarily a communication and coordination layer. A summary of a discussion does not automatically turn into a completed task, and teams still need a reliable process for assigning ownership and tracking delivery.

If your biggest problem is information scattered across conversations, Slack is worth considering. If the real bottleneck is executing engineering tasks, you'll probably need to pair it with a task management or agent execution system.

Explore Slack's AI capabilities.

3. ClickUp — Best for all-in-one project management

Best for: Teams that want tasks, documents, project views, and AI-assisted work in one platform.

ClickUp combines project management with documentation, task tracking, collaboration, and AI features. That makes it attractive to teams that would rather manage their work in one environment than maintain several separate applications.

A marketing team, for example, might use ClickUp to plan a campaign, assign content tasks, maintain documentation, and monitor deadlines. An engineering team can also use it to organize project work and track progress.

Key strengths

  • Multiple ways to view and organize work.
  • Tasks, documents, and project information in one platform.
  • AI assistance for supported writing, summarization, and productivity workflows.
  • Automation options for reducing repetitive project administration.

What to consider

An all-in-one platform can become complicated if the team configures too many spaces, custom fields, statuses, and workflows. AI features also vary by plan and availability, so check what is included before committing.

ClickUp is a good option when the main goal is consolidating project management and collaboration. Teams that need specialized AI-agent execution should separately evaluate how their coding tools fit into the workflow.

Explore ClickUp.

4. Notion — Best for documentation and shared knowledge

Best for: Teams that need a central place for project documentation, meeting notes, internal guides, and decisions.

Poor documentation creates collaboration problems that are easy to underestimate. People repeat questions, new teammates struggle to understand a project, and important decisions disappear inside old conversations.

Notion helps teams organize this information through shared pages, databases, wikis, and project workspaces. Its AI features can assist with tasks such as summarizing content, drafting documents, and finding information across supported sources.

Key strengths

  • Flexible documentation and knowledge management.
  • Shared project notes and internal wikis.
  • AI assistance for supported writing and information-retrieval tasks.
  • Connected documentation that teammates can update together.

What to consider

Notion works best when people maintain the information they put into it. An AI assistant cannot reliably compensate for outdated documentation, missing decisions, or inconsistent project records.

It can also be tempting to build an elaborate workspace when a simpler structure would be easier to maintain.

Choose Notion when the team needs a better source of truth for information, rather than another tool primarily focused on messaging or execution.

Explore Notion.

5. Asana — Best for cross-functional project coordination

Best for: Teams managing projects that involve multiple departments, stakeholders, and deadlines.

Some projects fail because the people doing the work are not communicating. Others fail because everyone is communicating, but nobody has a clear view of ownership, dependencies, and deadlines.

Asana focuses on the second problem.

It provides project and task management capabilities for organizing work, tracking progress, and connecting individual tasks to larger goals. Its AI features can support selected workflow and productivity tasks, depending on the plan and configuration.

For example, a product launch may involve design, engineering, marketing, and customer support. Each group has its own responsibilities, but the overall project depends on their work coming together at the right time.

Key strengths

  • Clear task ownership and deadlines.
  • Project views for monitoring progress.
  • Support for coordinating work across departments.
  • Workflow automation and AI-assisted productivity features.

What to consider

Asana is strongest when teams have defined projects and need a structured way to manage them. Teams should evaluate the available plans and AI features carefully, particularly if advanced automation or AI functionality is essential.

It is not primarily a coding-agent execution platform, so engineering teams with that requirement may need an additional tool.

Explore Asana.

6. Microsoft Teams — Best for organizations using Microsoft 365

Best for: Organizations that already use Microsoft tools for communication, documents, meetings, and business workflows.

Microsoft Teams brings chat, meetings, calls, and collaboration together. For organizations using Microsoft 365, its wider ecosystem can make it easier to connect conversations with shared files and workplace productivity tools.

Microsoft 365 Copilot adds AI assistance to supported experiences, helping eligible users work with meeting information, messages, documents, and other organizational context.

Key strengths

  • Meetings, messaging, and collaboration in one environment.
  • Integration with Microsoft 365 applications.
  • AI-assisted workflows through supported Copilot experiences.
  • Familiar collaboration options for organizations already invested in Microsoft.

What to consider

The experience depends on the organization's Microsoft 365 setup, licenses, and enabled features. Some AI capabilities require additional eligible subscriptions.

Teams may also find that adding AI features does not automatically improve collaboration if meetings lack clear outcomes or responsibilities remain undefined.

Microsoft Teams is a sensible choice when your company already runs on Microsoft 365 and wants to extend that environment rather than introduce an entirely new collaboration platform.

Explore Microsoft Teams.

7. Google Workspace — Best for real-time document collaboration

Best for: Teams that collaborate through shared documents, spreadsheets, presentations, email, and calendars.

Google Workspace is built around the idea that multiple people should be able to work on the same information without constantly sending files back and forth.

Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, and Gmail provide the foundation. Gemini features available through eligible Workspace plans can add AI assistance to supported workflows, including drafting, summarizing, and working with information.

This is particularly useful for distributed teams that prepare proposals, review reports, maintain shared spreadsheets, or collaborate on presentations.

Key strengths

  • Real-time collaboration on shared documents.
  • Straightforward file sharing and version history.
  • Connected email, calendar, storage, and productivity applications.
  • AI assistance in supported Workspace experiences.

What to consider

Google Workspace is primarily a productivity and collaboration ecosystem. It may not provide all the structured project management or specialized engineering execution features a team needs.

Also, check the current plan requirements for the Gemini features you intend to use. Availability and functionality can vary.

For teams that already work in Google Docs and Drive every day, improving the existing workflow may be more effective than moving everyone to a new platform.

Explore Google Workspace.

How to choose the right AI collaboration tool

The most useful tool is not necessarily the one with the largest list of AI features. It is the one that removes a recurring obstacle in your team's workflow.

Here is a practical way to narrow the options.

If your main challenge is… Start by evaluating…
Coordinating AI coding agents and engineering tasks Sharkly
Finding information in team conversations Slack
Managing projects and tasks in one workspace ClickUp
Keeping documentation and decisions organized Notion
Coordinating projects across departments Asana
Bringing AI into an existing Microsoft environment Microsoft Teams
Collaborating on documents and spreadsheets Google Workspace

Before choosing a tool, ask these questions:

1. Where does work currently get stuck?

Look for the actual bottleneck. It may be unclear ownership, scattered information, manual administration, or slow task execution. Choose a tool that addresses that problem directly.

2. Does the tool fit the team's existing workflow?

A platform can have impressive features and still fail if it forces the team to abandon useful habits or duplicate work across multiple systems.

3. What does the complete cost look like?

Consider user licenses, AI feature access, usage limits, integrations, and any model or API costs. A low starting price does not necessarily mean the full workflow will be inexpensive.

4. How will the team measure improvement?
