Pick a few concrete indicators, such as time spent searching for information, tasks completed on schedule, time from assignment to review, or the amount of repetitive administration.

5. Where does human review remain necessary?

AI can help with communication, planning, and execution, but teams still need people responsible for decisions, permissions, quality, and final approval.

Can one AI collaboration tool do everything?

Sometimes a single platform can cover most of a team's needs. But it is not always sensible to force communication, documentation, project management, and engineering execution into one application.

A practical setup might use Slack for communication, Notion for documentation, and a project management tool for task ownership. An engineering team working with multiple coding agents might add Sharkly to connect assigned work with agent execution and review.

The important thing is to avoid creating unnecessary overlap.

For example, if a team already has a project management platform it uses consistently, replacing it solely to gain an AI writing assistant may not be worthwhile. On the other hand, if coding agents are creating more work than the team can track, adding a coordination layer may address a more significant problem.

The goal is not to maximize the number of AI tools. It is to reduce the friction between deciding what needs to happen and getting that work completed.

Final thoughts

AI collaboration tools are most valuable when they improve a team's actual working process, not just its ability to generate text or summarize information.

Slack helps teams manage communication. Notion helps preserve knowledge. ClickUp and Asana organize projects. Microsoft Teams and Google Workspace extend AI assistance across familiar productivity environments.

For engineering teams adopting AI coding agents, Sharkly deserves particular attention because it connects task planning, agent assignment, execution visibility, and human review in one workflow. Instead of treating every coding agent as a separate tool to manage, teams can bring agent-driven work into the same system where they coordinate their projects.

My recommendation is to start with your biggest bottleneck, choose one tool that addresses it, and measure the result before expanding your stack. The best AI collaboration setup is the one that helps your team deliver better work with less coordination overhead.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best AI collaboration tool for teams in 2026?

It depends on the team's needs. Sharkly is worth evaluating for teams coordinating AI coding agents, Slack for communication, ClickUp for all-in-one project management, and Notion for shared documentation and knowledge.

Are AI collaboration tools suitable for small teams?

Yes. Small teams can use AI features to reduce repetitive work, organize projects, and share information more efficiently. However, it is worth checking free-plan limits, AI usage restrictions, and whether the tool adds unnecessary complexity.

Can AI collaboration tools replace project managers?

Not completely. They can assist with task tracking, summaries, reminders, and workflow automation, but people still need to set priorities, resolve conflicts, make decisions, and take responsibility for outcomes.

How is Sharkly different from an AI coding assistant?

An AI coding assistant or agent performs coding tasks. Sharkly focuses on coordinating the work around those agents: task assignment, context, progress, execution results, and human review. It connects to coding tools rather than replacing them.

Should a team use several AI collaboration tools together?

Yes, when each tool serves a distinct purpose and the integrations reduce rather than increase duplicated work. Start with a small set of complementary tools, establish clear ownership of information, and expand only when there is a demonstrated need.

articles.title: Durable execution for local LLM workflows: what I’m learning
articles.description: Most LLM demos assume the process stays alive. Kill it midway and the plan, the tool results, and the...
articles.body_html:
Most LLM demos assume the process stays alive. Kill it midway and the plan, the tool results, and the context all go with it. I've been spending time with a few tools that change that, and this is what I've picked up.

Durable execution changes how you think about failure

Temporal records every step of a workflow in an event history. If a worker dies, another one replays that history and continues from the last completed step. Finished work doesn't run twice.

For LLM workflows this maps well:

  • Model and tool calls belong in activities. They're slow, non-deterministic, and can fail, which is what activities are for.
  • Workflow code has to stay deterministic. Replay depends on it, so randomness, network calls, and timestamps stay out of it.
  • Retries become policy, not code. Backoff and timeouts are configuration instead of nested try/catch blocks.

Local models make failure cheap to test

Running a model through Ollama keeps the loop on your own machine. No rate limits, no API bill, and killing a process mid-run costs nothing. That makes it easy to test the unhappy path often, which is where most of the real bugs are.

The trade-off is that small local models are less predictable than hosted ones. Durable execution helps here because a bad step can be retried or inspected without redoing the whole run.

You can't trust what you can't see

Retries and resumes are invisible by default, and invisible failures are the hardest to debug. Sentry's tracing is a good fit, since a trace per step shows which call was slow, which one retried, and where a run picked back up.

A small React dashboard on top of the workflow history makes this easier still. Seeing a run's attempts as a timeline beats reading logs.

Open questions I'm still working through

  • How much state can sit in workflow history before replay gets slow?
  • Which failures should resume, and which should stop the run?
  • Does durability change how you write prompts and tool definitions?

I'll share more as I find answers.

articles.title: Microsoft’s 60,000-Employee Buyout Offer: What Should Developers Do in the AI Era?
articles.description: A headline about 60,000 employees is difficult to ignore.  For developers, it raises uncomfortable...
articles.body_html:
A headline about 60,000 employees is difficult to ignore.

For developers, it raises uncomfortable questions:

“Is my job becoming less secure?”

“Will knowing how to code still be enough?”

“Should I learn AI, change careers, or start building something of my own?”

Those questions deserve a practical answer. But first, we need to understand what Microsoft actually announced.

What Microsoft announced—and what it didn’t

On October 26, 2026, Microsoft announced a Voluntary Exit Offer for eligible employees in participating organizations.

The company said the program covers eligible employees at level 70 and below in Canada, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Participation varies by organization, and the offer includes financial support and career-planning resources.

Reuters reported that approximately 60,000 employees are eligible for the buyout offer.

Three distinctions matter:

  • This is a voluntary exit offer, rather than an announcement that 60,000 people have already been dismissed.
  • Eligible employees are not all developers.
  • The announcement does not establish that AI has replaced 60,000 jobs.

Microsoft’s statement describes adapting its workforce to changing needs. It does not provide a role-by-role explanation connecting departures to automation.

We should discuss the career implications without turning uncertainty into a dramatic claim.

Why developers are concerned anyway

Even with those distinctions, the news can feel unsettling.

You can spend years learning a stack, joining a respected company, and delivering good work—and still face changes outside your control.

A company may change its strategy, reduce a product’s scope, restructure teams, or redirect investment.

Individual ability matters, but employment decisions also reflect business priorities.

My takeaway from this announcement is that developers should build more career options. That is a practical response to uncertainty, not a prediction that software engineering is disappearing.

Here is what that looks like.

1. Learn to deliver with AI

Knowing how to ask an AI tool for a function is a starting point.

A more useful skill is taking a task from an unclear request to a working, verified result.

For example:

“Customers sometimes submit the same booking twice. Investigate the cause, implement a fix, and show how you verified it.”

Working through that task requires you to:

  • Understand the existing application.
  • Reproduce the problem.
  • Identify the relevant code.
  • Evaluate proposed changes.
  • Test duplicate and concurrent requests.
  • Explain what remains unverified.

AI can assist throughout the process. You still need to recognize whether the solution meets the requirement.

Practice complete workflows, including the parts after code generation.

Choose one tool and use it on a real project long enough to understand where it helps, where it struggles, and what information it needs.

2. Strengthen the fundamentals behind your framework

You don’t need to memorize every API.

You should be able to reason about the systems your code depends on.

A useful foundation includes:

Area Questions you should be able to investigate
Databases Why is this query slow? Can concurrent requests corrupt this operation?
Networking What does a timeout tell us? Is this operation safe to retry?
Security Can this user access this record? Where are permissions enforced?
Testing Does this test exercise the failure we care about?
Operations How will we detect a failure and recover from it?

Consider a payment bug.

An AI-generated patch might add retries. Understanding idempotency, transaction boundaries, and external side effects helps you decide whether those retries are safe.

Learn fundamentals through problems you can reproduce. Build a small example, break it, inspect the behavior, and explain the fix.

3. Connect your work to a business problem

Developers often describe their work in technical terms:

“I built a dashboard with React and PostgreSQL.”

That describes the implementation. It leaves the value unclear.

A more useful explanation is:

“I built a dashboard that lets a shop owner find unpaid repairs without checking paper tickets.”

Now someone understands why the software exists.

When starting a feature, ask:

  • Who needs this?
  • What are they doing today?
  • What goes wrong with that process?
  • What would improve if we solved it?
  • How could we check whether it helped?

You don’t need to become a salesperson to ask these questions. They help you choose what to build and explain your decisions.

Be careful with results. Claim time savings, revenue gains, or reduced errors only when you have evidence.

4. Build proof that someone else can inspect

A portfolio with ten nearly identical tutorial projects tells a limited story.

One well-explained project can reveal much more.

Include:

  • The problem and intended user.
  • A working demonstration.
  • Important technical decisions.
  • Tests tied to realistic failure cases.
  • Deployment instructions.
  • Known limitations.
  • What you would improve next.

For example, a booking app becomes more interesting when you explain how it handles two customers requesting the same slot.

A billing app becomes more credible when you show how payment status is reconciled after a timeout.

Let your portfolio demonstrate judgment as well as implementation.

If the project is a learning exercise, say so. You don’t need to invent users or revenue to make it valuable.

5. Develop knowledge of a specific domain

Technical skills become easier to apply when you understand the people using the software.

Choose an area you can investigate:

  • Repair shops.
  • Retail inventory.
  • Scheduling.
  • Logistics.
  • Property management.
  • Internal business reporting.

Talk to people who do the work. Learn their terminology, exceptions, and daily frustrations.

For a repair shop, you might discover that “completed” and “collected” are different states with different business consequences.

That detail affects the database, interface, reminders, and reports.

Domain knowledge helps you ask better questions before implementation. It also gives you something concrete to discuss with employers or customers.

6. Keep professional relationships active

If you are employed, you don’t have to begin a job search because of one headline.

You can still maintain your options:

  • Keep your résumé current.
  • Record completed work and its outcomes.
  • Stay in touch with former colleagues.
  • Share useful technical explanations.
  • Learn what roles in your target market require.

If you are looking for work, use job descriptions as evidence.

Review a manageable sample of relevant openings. Look for repeated requirements, then choose a few gaps to address.

Avoid rebuilding your entire learning plan around every tool that appears in one listing.

Relationships and visible work create opportunities to have more informed conversations. Neither guarantees an offer, but both give people a clearer picture of what you can do.

7. Explore paid work without treating it as an escape hatch

A side project can help you learn about customers and build an additional option.

It can also consume months without producing income.

Start with a small question:

“Can I solve one problem for one person who is willing to pay?”

That might lead to:

  • A fixed-scope automation project.
  • A reporting tool for a local business.
  • A small integration.
  • A paid setup service.
  • A focused software product.

Discuss the scope, price, support, and delivery expectations before building.

If you are employed, check applicable employment terms around outside work and intellectual property.

A business is an option to test. It should not be presented as a guaranteed solution to job insecurity.

A practical 30-day plan

You don’t need to learn everything at once. Choose one project and use it to build several connected skills.

Week 1: Choose a problem

Pick a customer or workflow you understand.

Write down the problem, expected behavior, and smallest useful result. Speak with potential users if the project is intended for sale.

For a career-focused project, compare the scope with the skills required in roles you want.

Week 2: Implement one complete workflow

Use AI to assist with investigation and implementation.

Keep changes small enough to inspect. Ask the tool to explain assumptions and identify missing information.

Make the main workflow work from beginning to end.

Week 3: Investigate failure cases

Test realistic problems:

  • Duplicate submissions.
  • Invalid inputs.
  • Unauthorized access.
  • Network failures.
  • Partial completion.

Choose the cases relevant to your project. Document how the system behaves.

Week 4: Make the work visible

Deploy a demonstration where appropriate.

Write a short case study explaining the problem, decisions, verification, and limitations.

Then use it in a concrete conversation: with a potential customer, a hiring team, a colleague, or a relevant community.

The goal after 30 days is a piece of work you understand and can defend.

What this announcement should change

Microsoft’s offer does not tell us exactly what the developer job market will look like next year.

It does give us a reason to examine how prepared we are for change.

Can you use AI productively?

Can you investigate a failure when generated code looks plausible?

Can you explain why a feature matters?

Can another person inspect evidence of your skills?

Those are useful questions whether you work at a large company, freelance, or build your own products.

You cannot control every restructuring decision. You can steadily improve your ability to solve problems, show your work, and pursue more than one opportunity.

What are you focusing on right now: AI-assisted development, stronger fundamentals, domain knowledge, or finding customers?

Sources

  • Microsoft: Introducing a Voluntary Exit Offer — October 26, 2026
  • Reuters: Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees

articles.title: I tested my browser-based email checkers against dkimpy, checkdmarc and pyspf: 12,618 results, 76 disagreements
articles.description: Five email security tools that run in the browser (DKIM, DMARC, SPF, MX and header analysis), each benchmarked against the Python library people already trust. Where we disagreed, who was right, and the bug the benchmark caught.
articles.body_html:
I built five email security tools for Toggle9 that run in the browser: a DKIM checker, a DMARC checker, an SPF checker, an MX lookup and an email header analyzer. There's no backend. DNS queries go from your browser to Cloudflare's public resolver, and DKIM signatures are verified with WebCrypto.

That raises an obvious question: why would anyone trust a JavaScript reimplementation of RFC 6376? There are established open-source libraries for all of this: dkimpy for DKIM, checkdmarc for DMARC and MX, pyspf (the reference implementation of RFC 7208) for SPF, and mail-parser for headers.

So I ran each tool against one of them, on real data, and read every result where they disagreed.

The scoreboard

Tool Reference Test set Compared Same answer
DKIM checker dkimpy 1.1.8 510 real emails from 18 public mailing lists 623 signatures 623
Email header analyzer mail-parser 4.8.0 The same 510 emails 2,333 hops 2,333
DMARC checker checkdmarc 5.17.2 747 popular domains (Tranco top 500 + top 250 .uk) 705 domains 692 (98.2%)
SPF checker pyspf 2.0.14 The first 200 of those domains that publish SPF 454 IP checks 451
MX lookup checkdmarc 5.17.2 746 domains 8,503 checks 8,443

That's 12,618 results and 76 disagreements. The benchmarks ran on 22 and 23 October 2026. The rest of this post is about those 76.

How a browser does DNS

Every tool here needs DNS: TXT records for SPF, DMARC and DKIM keys, MX records, and TLSA and PTR records. Browsers can't send raw DNS queries, but they can use DNS over HTTPS. Cloudflare's resolver answers JSON:

const r = await fetch(`https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=${encodeURIComponent(name)}&type=${type}`, {
  headers: { accept: 'application/dns-json' },
  referrerPolicy: 'no-referrer',
  credentials: 'omit',
});
const j = await r.json();
// j.Status: 0 = NOERROR, 3 = NXDOMAIN. j.Answer: [{ name, type, TTL, data }]

The real resolver adds a cache per check, a limit of six queries in flight, a 6-second timeout and one retry. An SPF check can fan out into dozens of lookups, so the cache matters more than you'd expect.

For DMARC, SPF and MX, my tools and the reference libraries queried the same resolver (1.1.1.1), so a difference can't be blamed on two resolvers seeing different DNS.

DKIM: 623 of 623, and why 65 signatures "failed"

DKIM verification is canonicalization (RFC 6376 section 3.4), then a hash, then a signature check. The relaxed header rule fits in a few lines:

export function canonHeader(raw, how) {
  if (how === 'simple') return raw + '\r\n';
  const i = raw.indexOf(':');
  const name = raw.slice(0, i).replace(/[ \t]+$/, '').toLowerCase();
  const val = raw.slice(i + 1).replace(/\r\n(?=[ \t])/g, '').replace(/[ \t]+/g, ' ').replace(/^ | $/g, '');
  return `${name}:${val}\r\n`;
}

WebCrypto handles both DKIM signing algorithms, RSA and Ed25519 (simplified):

if (alg === 'ed25519-sha256')
  return crypto.subtle.importKey('raw', pubKey, { name: 'Ed25519' }, false, ['verify']);
return crypto.subtle.importKey('spki', spki, { name: 'RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5', hash: 'SHA-256' }, false, ['verify']);

The test set was 510 recent posts to 18 public mailing lists, taken from lore.kernel.org's public git mirrors. They had 623 signatures from 57 domains; two of the signatures used Ed25519. dkimpy and my checker gave the same pass or fail on all 623.

The useful part was the 65 signatures that failed in both. A checker that just says "fail" isn't much help, so mine reads the receiving server's own Authentication-Results header (RFC 8601) to work out when the email changed:

  • 62 had passed when the email arrived, according to the receiving server. They were changed afterwards. In 60 of them, a signed List-Unsubscribe header was missing: the archive removes it before it publishes the email.
  • 3 had already failed on arrival. They were changed on the way.

So most of the "broken DKIM" in that set wasn't broken at delivery. It's what an archive does to an email. That's the line the tool shows: "The email was fine when it was delivered."

Email headers: 2,333 of 2,333

The header analyzer turns Received: headers into a route: which server handed the email to which, when, and how long each hop took. mail-parser parses the same headers. On the same 510 emails, both found the same number of hops in every email, and all 2,333 hops matched on server, time and delay.

DMARC: the benchmark caught my bug

The first DMARC run agreed on everything for 682 of 705 domains (96.7%). I read every difference, and the biggest group was mine to fix.

My checker called it an error when an SPF record reached the same include: from two branches. msn.com, doi.org, grammarly.com and 7 others do this. I'd treated a repeat as a loop. Nothing in RFC 7208 makes a repeated include an error. Real loops get caught by the 10-lookup limit, and a repeat just counts against that limit. The fix: follow the repeat, count it again, and show a warning.

The second run agreed on 692 of 705 (98.2%). I read the 13 that were left by hand, against the RFCs:

Domains What happened Who's right
www.gov.uk, legislation.gov.uk, account.gov.uk, data.gov.uk No DMARC record of their own. The parent gov.uk record's sp=none applies to subdomains (RFC 9989). Mine
gcdn.co, thomsonreuters.co.uk SPF includes a name that doesn't exist in DNS, which is a permerror (RFC 7208 section 5.2) Mine
weather.com An unrelated TXT record at _dmarc alongside the real one; checkdmarc rejects it Mine
autodesk.com An = in the local part of a ruf address, which the standard allows Mine
alibabadns.com v=SPF1 in capitals. The ABNF is case-insensitive. Mine
globo.com rua=mailto: dmarc@… with a space. Both call the address invalid; checkdmarc then rejects the whole record, but RFC 9989 keeps p=none. Mine
iiko.it, who.int 15 and 17 DNS lookups (iiko.it confirmed by hand through 1.1.1.1). checkdmarc stops counting early. Mine
ozon.ru checkdmarc timed out Neither

"Mine" is my reading of the standards, written up with the RFC section each time. You don't have to take my word for it: the domains are real, so you can check them.

None of this makes checkdmarc a bad library. Rejecting a record the standards would accept is a reasonable choice for a tool that audits your own domain. Mine follows the standards' wording, because its job is to explain what a receiver should do with the record.

SPF: 451 of 454, and the 3 that weren't real

For each of 200 domains, I tested up to four IP addresses: the domain's own mail server, an address inside a range its record lists, an address reserved for documentation that never sends email, and a Google sending address for domains that include Google.

Three results differed: youtube.com, archive.org and youtube-nocookie.com, all for the same Google address. Large providers' DNS answers rotate, so an address can be listed in one lookup and missing from the next. Run again side by side, both tools agreed on all three.

MX: 8,443 of 8,503, and the rotation problem

The MX lookup checks a lot per domain: the MX hosts, their addresses, reverse DNS (PTR) and whether it points back, TLSA (DANE) records, MTA-STS and TLS reporting. Across 746 domains that came to 8,503 comparisons.

MX host sets matched on all 746 domains. MTA-STS and TLS reporting matched on all 746 too.

The addresses were the hard part. 738 of the 1,246 mail servers answered with a different few of their addresses each time. Google, Microsoft and Proofpoint spread their load that way, so two lookups a few minutes apart rarely agree, from any tool. Comparing those sets directly would only measure luck.

So the benchmark asks each server again over a few seconds. If those lookups turn up every address either tool saw, the server counts as rotating and isn't compared. That left 508 servers with steady answers, and 458 matched exactly. Of the 50 that didn't, 47 are Google or Proofpoint servers of the same rotating kind, whose other address didn't turn up in those few seconds.

The remaining 10 were differences in records. On 26 October I checked each one by hand through 1.1.1.1. In every case, the record my tool found is there:

  • TLSA: mx.ietf.org, two comcast.net servers and cm.com's Microsoft server publish TLSA records. checkdmarc reported none.
  • PTR: three servers (nic.ru, debian.org, ebi.ac.uk) have reverse DNS. checkdmarc reported none.
  • Forward-confirmed PTR: two huawei.com names do resolve back to their addresses.
  • Addresses: one Outlook server has IPv6 addresses that checkdmarc didn't list.

What I'd tell anyone writing a benchmark like this

  1. A reference library is a witness, not a judge. If you count disagreements as your failures, you end up copying the library's choices. Read each one against the spec.
  2. Read every difference, especially at the start. My first DMARC run had a real bug hiding behind a 96.7% score that looked fine.
  3. Handle rotating answers before comparing. Otherwise you're measuring DNS load balancing, not your code.
  4. Tie the results to the code. Each tool's test file hashes its engine and compares that with the hash stored in its benchmark result. Change the DKIM verifier without re-running the benchmark, and npm test fails: 
test('dkim-bench.json was made by the engine that ships', () => {
  const b = JSON.parse(readFileSync(new URL('dkim-bench.json', dir), 'utf8'));
  const h = createHash('sha256')
    .update(readFileSync(new URL('verify.js', dir)))
    .update(readFileSync(new URL('compute.js', dir)))
    .digest('hex').slice(0, 16);
  assert.equal(b.engine, h);
});

So the numbers quoted on each tool's page can't silently drift away from the code.

Try them

All five run in your browser, with no account. When you check a domain, only the DNS names go to Cloudflare's public resolver. Headers and emails you paste are read on your device.

  • DKIM checker
  • DMARC checker
  • SPF checker
  • MX lookup
  • Email header analyzer

If you check DMARC for a living, I'd like to hear where you think I've read RFC 9989 wrong, especially on those 13.

articles.title: How we built an MCP App for a cash-on-delivery store in Uzbekistan
articles.description: By the Birinchi Shop team  In Uzbekistan most online shopping still ends with cash. You pick a...
articles.body_html:
By the Birinchi Shop team

In Uzbekistan most online shopping still ends with cash. You pick a product, leave your name and phone number, a call-center operator phones you to confirm, and a courier brings the parcel 1–3 days later. You inspect it at the door and pay the courier in cash, or refuse it.

Birinchi Shop works exactly like that, with 300+ products and delivery to every region of the country. Recently we gave the store a public MCP server, so an AI assistant can search the catalog and place an order for a shopper. This week we turned it into an MCP App. Instead of a wall of JSON-ish text, the assistant now shows real product cards, a variant picker and an order form, right inside the chat.

This post covers how it is built and what broke when we first tried it in a real host.

The starting point: a small, stateless MCP server

Our shop server is deliberately boring. It runs on Express, with no SDK: one POST endpoint that speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over Streamable HTTP. It keeps no sessions, needs no API key and uses no SSE stream. It exposes five tools:

Tool What it does
search_products keyword search over the catalog (Uzbek/Russian names), price filters
get_product images, video, variants with their own price and stock, total to pay
store_info delivery area, fee, cash-on-delivery, returns
place_order places a real order that a call center will phone
get_order_status needs the order id and the last 4 digits of the phone

place_order is the dangerous one, because every order costs a real operator's phone call. So the server enforces rules no matter what the model does:

  • customer_confirmed: true is required. Without it the call is rejected with a message telling the agent to ask the shopper first.
  • The phone must be a valid Uzbek mobile number.
  • The same limits as our website apply: one order per phone per product per 24 hours, at most three different products.
  • There is a per-IP hourly cap and a daily cap for the whole AI channel.
  • Every AI order is flagged for the admins.

Cash on delivery helps a lot here. Even if something goes wrong, nobody gets charged. A bad order costs us one phone call.

What an MCP App adds

The MCP Apps extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui) lets a tool point at an HTML resource. A host that supports it renders that HTML in a sandboxed iframe next to the tool result. The view and the host talk JSON-RPC over postMessage.

There are three pieces on the server side.

1. Tools point at a ui:// resource

const APP_URI = 'ui://birinchi-shop/store-v4.html';

const uiMeta = (invoking, invoked) => ({
  ui: { resourceUri: APP_URI },                          // MCP Apps standard
  'openai/outputTemplate': 'ui://birinchi-shop/store-v4.skybridge.html', // ChatGPT Apps SDK
  'openai/widgetAccessible': true,
  'openai/toolInvocation/invoking': invoking,
  'openai/toolInvocation/invoked': invoked,
});

// in the tool list:
{ name: 'search_products', _meta: uiMeta('Searching the store…', 'Products found'), ... }

Four of the five tools share one view: search, product, order and status. store_info stays text-only.

2. The resource itself

case 'resources/read': {
  const r = APP_RESOURCES.find(x => x.uri === msg.params?.uri);
  if (!r) return rpcError(msg.id, -32002, 'Resource not found');
  return rpcResult(msg.id, { contents: [{
    uri: r.uri,
    mimeType: r.mimeType,           // 'text/html;profile=mcp-app'
    text: readAppHtml(),
    _meta: {
      ui: { csp: { resourceDomains: ['https://birinchishop.uz'], connectDomains: [] },
            prefersBorder: false },
    },
  }] });
}

The CSP is tight. The view may load images and video from our own domain and nothing else, and it makes no network requests at all. Every call to the server goes through the host as tools/call.

3. The text result does not change

The tool still returns content (text) and structuredContent (JSON). Clients without UI support keep working exactly as before. The view just reads structuredContent.

One HTML file, no build step

The view is a single ~45 KB HTML file with inline CSS and JS: no framework, no bundler, no CDN. It works out what to render from the shape of the result:

function showResult(res) {
  const sc = res.structuredContent;
  if (res.isError || !sc)                       return showError(res);
  if (Array.isArray(sc.items))                  return showList(sc);      // search_products
  if (sc.total_to_pay && Array.isArray(sc.variants)) return openProduct(sc); // get_product
  if ('next_steps' in sc && 'order_id' in sc)   return showDone(sc);      // place_order
  if (sc.status_text)                           return showStatus(sc);    // get_order_status
}

Product names come from our database and some of them are messy, so all text goes into the DOM through textContent and a tiny h(tag, attrs, ...children) helper. There is no innerHTML anywhere.

The bridge itself is small: send ui/initialize, store hostContext (theme, CSS variables, locale, display mode), send ui/notifications/initialized, then listen for ui/notifications/tool-result. A ResizeObserver reports ui/notifications/size-changed, so the iframe grows when the shopper opens the order form.

Tapping a card calls get_product from the view. The model is not involved, so browsing is instant and costs no tokens.

Consent belongs in the UI

In the text-only version the model had to collect name, phone and region in chat, read the total back and get a "yes". That works, but it is easy to get wrong, and a confirmation the model typed for the shopper is still just text.

In the app, the shopper fills in the form themselves. The next screen repeats the product, variant, name, phone, region and the cash total, and has one button: "I confirm — place order". Only that tap sends place_order with customer_confirmed: true. The server-side rules still apply on top.

After a successful order the view calls ui/update-model-context, so the assistant knows the order already exists and does not place it again:

bridge.updateContext(
  `The shopper placed order #${o.order_id} in the store app ... Do not place this order again.`,
  { order_id: o.order_id, status: o.status }
);

get_order_status renders as a simple timeline: received → operator confirms → with the courier → delivered, paid in cash.

Four bugs that only showed up in the real host

Everything passed in our local harness, a headless Chrome page that iframes the view and plays the host. Then we opened it on a phone in Claude.

1. clientInfo vs appInfo

The first live run showed our fallback error screen. We had written the ui/initialize params from memory, MCP-style, with clientInfo. The view protocol uses appInfo:

await request('ui/initialize', {
  protocolVersion: '2026-01-26',
  appInfo: { name: 'birinchi-shop-app', version: '1.1.0' },   // not clientInfo
  appCapabilities: { availableDisplayModes: ['inline', 'fullscreen'] },
});

Our harness answered any ui/initialize; the real host validated the params. Lesson: copy the request shape from the SDK's types (spec.types.ts in the ext-apps repo), and make the error screen print the actual reason. We now show it in brackets, so a screenshot is enough to debug.

2. A white card in a dark chat

Next, the view rendered in a dark chat with a white background and washed-out green text. The host passes theme variables as light-dark(#fff, #262624). light-dark() resolves from the element's color-scheme, and we never set one, so it always picked the light value. Meanwhile our own accent colors followed data-theme="dark", hence the odd mix.

3. ...and then a black frame around it

The fix for #2 was color-scheme: dark on :root. That made things worse in a different way. When an iframe's root color-scheme differs from its embedding page, the browser paints the iframe with an opaque canvas background, and a dark rectangle appeared around our card. The final version sets color-scheme on the app container instead of the root, so the iframe stays transparent and the host variables resolve correctly:

#app { color-scheme: light; color: var(--fg); }
:root[data-theme="dark"] #app { color-scheme: dark; }

4. Hosts cache the resource

After every HTML change, the phone kept showing the old version. Hosts cache ui:// resources, so we now put a version in the URI (store-v4.html) and bump it with every change to the view. Reconnecting the connector refreshes the tool list.

A bonus trap, specific to our setup: the Puppeteer in our frontend was so old that its bundled Chromium could not parse optional chaining (?.). The harness has to use a current Chrome, or it reports syntax errors no real user will ever see.

Testing without creating orders

Every real place_order rings a real phone, so the server accepts one reserved reviewer number. That number runs all the validation (product exists, in stock, variant chosen, valid phone) but returns test: true and never creates an order. The view shows a "Test order" screen for it. Directory reviewers get the number in our submission notes, and it is how we test on production.

The harness itself is under 100 lines: a page with an iframe, a fake host that answers ui/initialize, forwards tools/call to the real server handler, and resizes the iframe on size-changed. A script then clicks through search → product → variant → form → confirm and takes screenshots in light and dark mode.

What we would tell someone starting today

  • Keep the text result first-class. The UI is an extra layer; plenty of clients will never render it.
  • Let the view call your tools directly for browsing. It is faster and keeps the model out of simple clicks.
  • Put irreversible actions behind a button the user taps, and still enforce the rules on the server.
  • Lock the CSP down and route all data through tools/call.
  • Version your ui:// URIs.
  • Test in a real host early, on a phone, in dark mode.

If you want to see it working, add our store server as a custom connector in an MCP client that supports apps:

https://birinchishop.uz/api/shop/mcp

No API key is needed. Ask for something like "find a watch in Birinchi Shop". The usage guide is at birinchishop.uz/en/ai-shopping.

Questions about the implementation are welcome in the comments.

articles.title: Halftone type in WebGL, one draw call per headline
articles.description: Every large title on this site is drawn as halftone dots. They fly in and assemble after the...
articles.body_html:
Every large title on this site is drawn as halftone dots. They fly in and assemble after the preloader, push away from the cursor and scatter as you scroll. It looks like an image effect, but the text is real: you can select it, search it, and a screen reader reads it like any other heading. This note covers how that works and what it costs.

Keep the text, paint over it

The component, DotText, renders the heading as normal HTML and lays a canvas over it. Once the WebGL scene is ready the element gets an is-live class, which makes the glyphs transparent while keeping them in the DOM. If WebGL is missing, the context is lost or the page runs in forced-colours mode, the canvas is hidden and an SVG filter draws a static halftone instead. Without JavaScript you get that static version too.

That split decides most of the rest: layout, wrapping and font loading all belong to CSS, and the canvas only has to copy what the browser already laid out.

Sampling the glyphs the browser drew

Rendering the string again with fillText would wrap and kern differently from the DOM. So the sampler walks the element’s text nodes and uses a Range to read each character’s client rect. Each glyph is drawn on an offscreen 2D canvas at exactly that position, with a horizontal scale that matches the DOM advance in case the canvas picks a slightly different width.

The display face is a variable font set to a condensed width, and canvas fonts don’t take font-variation-settings. The closest you get is ctx.fontStretch, so the computed font-stretch percentage is mapped to the nearest keyword (extra-condensed for this face).

From coverage to dot sizes

The alpha channel of that canvas is the ink coverage. Two box-blur passes per axis approximate a gaussian, so coverage falls off smoothly at the edge of each stroke. A grid is then laid over the result, and each cell becomes one dot whose radius follows the blurred coverage under it:

const r = (pitch / 2) * Math.min(0.92, v * 0.8 - 0.08)
if (r < 0.35) continue // too small to see; skip the point entirely
home.push(x - pad, y - pad)
rs.push(r)

Dots are full inside a stroke and shrink towards its edge, the same screen the SVG fallback produces, so the two versions match. The grid pitch is 6px on desktop and 4px below 720px, where type is smaller and needs a finer screen to stay readable.

All the motion lives in the vertex shader

Each dot gets its home position, radius and four random numbers as attributes, uploaded once. Everything that moves is a uniform: intro progress, scroll scatter, time and the cursor position. The vertex shader works out each dot’s position from those, so a frame is a handful of uniform* calls and one drawArrays(gl.POINTS), whether the title has 2,000 dots or 20,000.

// Intro: each dot flies in from its own offset with its own delay
float t = clamp(uProgress * 1.8 - aRand.w * 0.8, 0.0, 1.0);
float e = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - t, 3.0);
vec2 pos = uOrigin + aHome + aRand.xy * uSpread * (0.4 + aRand.w) * (1.0 - e);

// Cursor repulsion
vec2 d = pos - uMouse;
float len = length(d);
float f = (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, uRadius, len)) * uMouseStrength;
pos += d / max(len, 0.001) * f * uPush;

The fragment shader draws an anti-aliased disc from gl_PointCoord and blends towards the accent colour by how hard the cursor is pushing that dot. Colour is read from the element’s computed color, so theme switches and hover transitions carry over without extra code.

Building lazily

Sampling is the expensive part: reading pixels back and blurring them is main-thread work. The first version built every title on load, including the footer, and it showed up as long tasks. Now an IntersectionObserver with a half-viewport margin decides when a title is near enough to sample, and the ticker skips titles that are off-screen or in a hidden tab. A ResizeObserver and document.fonts.ready mark the scene dirty, and it rebuilds on the next frame only if it is near the viewport.

Under prefers-reduced-motion the dots are drawn once, at rest, and repainted only when the colour changes. No ticker runs at all.

What I would keep

  • Leave the text in the DOM. The effect is decoration on top of a heading, and it never replaces one.
  • Sample what the browser rendered instead of re-implementing text layout.
  • Put the per-frame work in a shader and keep the CPU side to uniforms.
  • Do the costly setup only when the element is about to be seen.

Originally published on my site. I'm Muhammad Tanveer, a full-stack developer in Faisalabad, Pakistan: muhammad-tanveer-dev.vercel.app.

articles.title: From client-only to SSR: building Gemkit, a SvelteKit-style framework for Web Components
articles.description: How I added SSR and hydration to the Gem Web Components library, built an app framework on Rsbuild, and benchmarked it against SvelteKit, Nuxt and Next.js.
articles.body_html:
A long time ago I built Gem, a library for building UI components and apps with Web Components. It was pleasant to use, but it had one big weakness: client-side rendering only. Even GemBook, its documentation site generator, rendered everything in the browser, so search engines saw an almost empty HTML page.

This post is about how I brought Gem to the server: first a gem-ssr prototype on jsdom that could serialize and hydrate, then moving away from jsdom and isolating requests, and finally Gemkit, an app framework inspired by Next.js and SvelteKit. At the end, I compare it with SvelteKit, Nuxt and Next.js using the RealWorld app.

Why SSR is hard for Web Components

React and Vue components are framework abstractions, so the server can turn a virtual DOM into a string. Web Components are different, they depend on the browser:

  • Elements are class extends HTMLElement, which needs customElements, HTMLElement, document...
  • Styles and content live in Shadow DOM, which plain HTML could not express
  • Gem templates are based on (a modified) lit-html, which renders real DOM nodes, not a virtual DOM

Fortunately, Declarative Shadow DOM is now supported by all major browsers: <template shadowrootmode="open"> puts Shadow DOM directly in HTML. The remaining question was how to run Gem elements in Node.js.

The prototype: serialization and hydration on jsdom

The most direct idea: Gem needs a DOM, so give it one. The first version of gem-ssr used jsdom to emulate the browser and got the core of SSR working:

1. Serialization. Elements are created and rendered on the server, then serialized to HTML together with their Shadow DOM, output as Declarative Shadow DOM. The browser can display the page right away.

2. Hydration. The server output contains comment markers for each template binding. When an element renders on the client for the first time, it uses the markers to connect bindings to the existing DOM. It only attaches event listeners and sets properties, it doesn't recreate the DOM. Templates also carry a digest; on a mismatch, the client warns and re-renders only that part.

That proved SSR with Web Components works. But jsdom was far from production ready:

  • jsdom is heavy, every request goes through a full DOM implementation
  • There is only one global document, location and history, so concurrent requests pollute each other

gem-ssr: dropping jsdom, isolating requests

Next, I moved gem-ssr towards production:

1. Render to strings without jsdom. gem-ssr provides only the minimal DOM Gem needs and compiles templates to strings on the server. The serialization and hydration protocol stays the same.

2. Request isolation. With AsyncLocalStorage, stores, history, location and the i18n language are scoped per request.

3. Streaming. render returns an async iterable. Content before pending async elements is sent first, and independent async elements are awaited in parallel:

import { render } from '@mantou/gem-ssr';

const stream = ReadableStream.from(render(html`<app-root></app-root>`, { url: req.url }));

At this point gem-ssr could run in a real server. But routing, data loading, forms and deployment still had to be assembled by every project. That's what Gemkit is for.

Gemkit: the app framework for Gem

Gemkit borrows heavily from Next.js and SvelteKit: file-based routing, layouts, load, form actions, SSR/SSG/ISR. It is an Rsbuild plugin, so Rsbuild's config, dev server and plugins all keep working.

npm create gemkit@latest my-app

One file is one page 

// src/pages/index.ts
@page('Home')
export default class HomePage extends GemElement {
  @template()
  #content = () => html`<h1>Hello Gemkit</h1>`;
}

No @customElement needed, the tag name comes from the file path, and Gem and common Gemkit APIs are auto-imported. This page is prerendered to dist/web/index.html at build time and hydrated on the client.

For Gemkit, unplugin-gem also got an ssr option: its swc plugin adds a key to module-level createStore calls based on the file path and variable name, so client and server builds agree. Stores updated during server rendering are output by key, and the client uses those values, so the first render matches the HTML.

The project structure will look familiar if you know SvelteKit:

src/
  app.ts               global styles, stores
  app.server.ts        handle: runs before each server request
  elements/            app-* elements, auto-imported
  pages/
    _layout.ts         root layout, <gemkit-outlet> renders child routes
    _error.ts          error page / 404
    index.ts           /
    blog/
      _layout.ts       nested layout, kept while navigating within /blog/*
      [slug].ts        /blog/:slug
      [slug].server.ts server-only load / actions
      [...rest].ts     /blog/*
  locales/
    en.json            default language
    zh.json            /zh/*

Data loading: isomorphic load + server modules

A page's load is isomorphic: it runs during SSR and client navigation. Server-only code goes in a *.server.ts file with the same name. It's never bundled for the client; importing it from client code fails the build:

// src/pages/blog/[slug].server.ts
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

export async function load({ params }) {
  return { markdown: await readFile(`content/${params.slug}.md`, 'utf8') };
}

// src/pages/blog/[slug].ts
@page<{ slug: string }, { markdown: string }>({
  load: ({ data }) => parseMarkdown(data.markdown),
  title: ({ data }) => data.title,
})
export default class PostPage extends GemElement {
  @property data?: { html: string };

  @template()
  #content = () => html`<article .innerHTML=${this.data?.html}></article>`;
}
  • First load: data is embedded in the HTML as JSON and used during hydration, no extra request
  • Client navigation: Gemkit fetches <page path>/__data.json with the data of the page and all its layouts
  • Prerendering: data files are written next to pages, so client navigation works on static hosting too

Requests, cookies, redirects and forms

In *.server.ts, load can read the request and cookies and redirect in one line, and actions handle form submissions, just like SvelteKit:

// src/pages/article/[slug].server.ts (from the RealWorld app)
export async function load(ctx) {
  const [{ article }, { comments }] = await Promise.all([
    api(ctx, `articles/${ctx.params.slug}`),
    api(ctx, `articles/${ctx.params.slug}/comments`),
  ]);
  // markdown is converted on the server, marked and sanitize-html never reach the client
  return { article: { ...article, body: sanitizeHtml(await marked(article.body)) }, comments };
}

export const actions = {
  deleteArticle: async (ctx) => {
    await api(ctx, `articles/${ctx.params.slug}`, 'DELETE');
    redirect(303, '/');
  },
};

API routes are plain *.server.ts modules exporting GET, POST, etc., with a typed $gemkit/api client.

Server elements: islands with Web Components

This is where Gemkit and Web Components fit together best. A page can mix three kinds of elements:

Decorator Server Client
@server() rendered no code, no hydration; code and dependencies stay out of the client bundle
@lazy({ on }) rendered shows server HTML, loads code and hydrates on interaction / visible / idle
@client() tag only renders normally, the module can use browser-only code 
@customElement('app-like-button')
@lazy({ on: 'interaction' })
class AppLikeButtonElement extends GemElement {}

By default @lazy loads on the first interaction, and the event that triggered loading (click, pointerdown, etc.) is re-dispatched to the original target, so the first click is not lost. Rarely used parts like like-buttons and comment boxes don't cost first-load JS.

@server() can also mark a method or field. It runs during SSR, the resulting state is output with the element and restored during hydration, and the first run on the client is skipped, so data isn't fetched twice:

@customElement('app-comments')
class AppCommentsElement extends GemElement {
  #state = createState({ comments: [] as Comment[] });

  // Server: awaited before output, state is sent with the element
  // Client: restored on first load and skipped; runs when mounted after client navigation
  @server()
  @mounted()
  #load = async () => this.#state({ comments: await fetchComments() });

  @template()
  #content = () => html`${this.#state.comments.map((c) => html`<p>${c.text}</p>`)}`;
}

Rendering modes: SSG, SSR, ISR

  • Every page is prerendered at build time by default (SSG) and can be deployed to any static host
  • Pages that read cookies or the request export prerender = false and are rendered per request by gemkit start
  • export const revalidate = 60 enables ISR: rendered and cached on the first request, then re-rendered in the background when stale

Also: links prefetch modules, data and server element HTML on hover; back/forward restores from a history cache without requests and restores scroll position; src/locales generates locale-prefixed routes.

GemBook now runs on Gemkit, so Gem's documentation sites finally have full SSR/SSG. The Gemkit docs are built with it.

RealWorld comparison

To check whether Gemkit holds up in a real app, I implemented RealWorld (Conduit, a Medium clone) and compared it with the SvelteKit, Nuxt and Next.js implementations on the same local backend, seed data and theme CSS.

Apple M2, 16 GB, Node v25.8.1, Lighthouse median of 5 runs.

Client JS (gzip)

Home Article JS requests (home)
Gemkit 25.9 KB 25.9 KB 2
SvelteKit 44.0 KB 43.3 KB 23
Nuxt 85.8 KB 85.5 KB 15
Next.js 103.5 KB 126.5 KB 8

Lighthouse, home (mobile, simulated throttling)

Score FCP LCP TBT
Gemkit 100 906 ms 1361 ms 0
SvelteKit 100 1285 ms 1671 ms 0
Nuxt 99 1656 ms 1806 ms 0
Next.js 96 908 ms 2022 ms 4

SSR throughput (autocannon, 20 connections, median of 5 rounds)

Home req/s Article req/s
Gemkit 1382 1377
SvelteKit 1437 1388
Nuxt 1042 1169
Next.js 317 359

Other

Client navigation (home → article) Source lines Official e2e passed
Gemkit 53 ms 968 84 / 91
SvelteKit 78 ms 1143 6 / 93
Nuxt 95 ms 711 86 / 91
Next.js 86 ms 2712 60 / 91

How to read this:

  • JS size: Gemkit's home page ships about 59% of SvelteKit's JS, 30% of Nuxt's and 25% of Next's. Web Components are a browser feature, so the framework runtime is small.
  • Lighthouse: Gemkit and SvelteKit both score 100; Gemkit's FCP is about 400 ms faster.
  • SSR throughput: Gemkit and SvelteKit are roughly even (SvelteKit is 1–4% higher), 18–33% above Nuxt and about 4x Next. Both are close to the shared backend's limit; Gemkit spent about 44% of the time waiting for the backend.
  • e2e: the remaining Gemkit failures are mostly environment issues (slow external images, the backend only returning popular tags). The SvelteKit and Next community implementations predate the e2e conventions (different routes), so their low pass rates don't mean missing features.

Building RealWorld was also a good round of dogfooding. It exposed and fixed several issues: load couldn't access the request, query-only navigation didn't re-run load, and children hydrating before their parents caused mismatches. CPU profiling found that every route match created a new URLPattern (now cached, with plain string comparison for patterns without parameters) and an extra TextEncoderStream. After those fixes, home page throughput went from 661 to about 1380 req/s.

Code, reproduction steps and raw data are on GitHub. Corrections are welcome.

Summary

Gem went from client-only to a full SSR framework in three steps:

  1. jsdom prototype: serialization (Declarative Shadow DOM) and hydration without recreating the DOM, proving SSR works for Web Components
  2. gem-ssr: no jsdom, string rendering + request isolation + streaming
  3. Gemkit: on top of gem-ssr and inspired by Next.js / SvelteKit, with file-based routing, layouts, load/actions, server elements, SSG/ISR and i18n

The result is a framework built on web standards, with ~26 KB of first-load JS and performance on par with SvelteKit. If you're interested in Web Components, give it a try:

npm create gemkit@latest my-app
  • GitHub: https://github.com/mantou132/gem
  • Gemkit docs: https://gemkit.gemjs.org/en/
  • Gem docs: https://gemjs.org

articles.title: O fantasma que assombra o PDF da Fecombustíveis: um robô que transforma a tributação dos combustíveis em XML
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

Transparência antes de tudo: este projeto usa o Google Gemini (API fechada) para ler o PDF — não um modelo open-weight. Conto abaixo por que fiz essa escolha, onde o código é aberto e o que falta para trocar por um modelo aberto.

What I Built

Todo mês, sem aviso de horário, aparece um PDF no site da Fecombustíveis: a "Carga tributária estadual" dos combustíveis. Ali estão o PMPF, a alíquota de ICMS, o tributo estadual e o federal de gasolina, diesel, etanol e GNV para as 27 UFs.

Quem emite nota fiscal de combustível no Brasil precisa desses números para a Lei da Transparência (o "valor aproximado dos tributos" no cupom). No nosso caso, eles alimentam o XML TransparenciaTributos usado no nosso sistema de emissão fiscal. Antes, alguém abria o PDF — com as tabelas em imagem — e digitava dezenas de valores à mão.

O Transparência de Tributos – Combustíveis é o "fantasma na máquina" que faz isso sozinho:

  • 👻 Assombra a página da Fecombustíveis a cada 8 horas procurando o PDF novo;
  • 📄 Lê o PDF com IA e devolve os valores por combustível e UF;
  • 🧮 Confere as contas (PMPF × alíquota = ICMS; no GNV, PMPF × 9,25% = PIS/COFINS) e se recusa a gravar se algo não fechar;
  • 🕯️ Honra o passado: o bloco de vigência antigo não é apagado — ele "termina" no dia anterior (ex.: até 30/09/2026) e nasce um bloco novo (01/10/2026 até 2050). O histórico de cada tributo fica preservado no XML;
  • 🔔 Avisa por e-mail e no Discord quando a tributação muda;
  • 🌐 Publica uma página pública com os tributos por estado.

Minha leitura do tema: o PDF mensal é um fantasma que aparece quando quer, e a ideia foi deixar a máquina vigiando por mim — sem perder a memória dos meses anteriores, que é o que o fisco pede quando confere uma nota antiga.

Demo

  • Gerador (passos 1–3): https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/
  • Tributos por estado: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/tributos.html

Fluxo no site:

  1. Passo 1 – o PDF mais recente já vem selecionado, com o XML do mês anterior como base.
  2. Passo 2 – a IA extrai os valores; o que mudou fica amarelo (com o valor antigo embaixo) e conta que não fecha ganha borda vermelha. Tudo é editável na tabela.
  3. Passo 3 – Gerar XML, Baixar XML e, se quiser, Baixar Excel.

Code

imextecnologia / tributacao

tributacao

Transparência de Tributos – Combustíveis

Site estático (GitHub Pages) que gera todo mês o XML TransparenciaTributos a partir do PDF "Carga tributária estadual" da Fecombustíveis.

Site: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/ · Tributos por estado: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/tributos.html

Como funciona

  1. Busca do PDF – a cada 8 horas um workflow procura o PDF novo na página da Fecombustíveis, salva em pdf/ e já gera o XML do mês em xml/ (veja Busca automática do PDF).
  2. Leitura com IA – o site envia o PDF ao Google Gemini, que devolve os valores por combustível e UF.
  3. Comparação – os valores são comparados com o XML do mês anterior (em xml/) e o que mudou fica destacado.
  4. Geração – para cada combustível que mudou, o bloco antigo termina no dia anterior (ex.: 30/09/2026) e é criado um bloco novo (ex.: 01/10/2026 até 01/01/2050). Combustíveis sem mudança ficam como estão Também é possível baixar uma planilha…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Sem servidor. É um site estático no GitHub Pages; tudo roda no navegador ou num job do GitHub Actions.

Busca automática (.github/workflows/buscar-pdf.yml, cron 0 */8 * * *):

  1. scripts/buscar-pdf.js lê a página da Fecombustíveis e pega o link do PDF mais recente pela data no nome ("10 OUTUBRO 2026" vem antes de "01 OUTUBRO 2026"). Se a página falhar, tenta o link no padrão do mês atual e do próximo.
  2. scripts/gerar-xml.js gera o XML do PDF novo usando o mesmo prompt, produtos e UFs do index.html — o script extrai essas constantes direto do HTML, então site e robô nunca divergem.
  3. scripts/buscar-painel.js relê o quadro oficial de percentuais e atualiza painel.json.
  4. Se algo mudou: commit, publicação do site e aviso por e-mail/Discord com o diff.

A IA. O PDF vai para o Gemini com um prompt que pede somente JSON num formato fixo (gasolina/diesel com valor único; etanol e GNV por UF). O site tenta uma lista de modelos em ordem (gemini-flash-latest → gemini-flash-lite-latest → gemini-2.5-flash → gemini-2.5-flash-lite), com nova tentativa em 429/503.

A rede de segurança importa mais que o modelo. IA lendo tabela em imagem erra dígito. Por isso:

// PMPF × alíquota precisa bater com o ICMS (etanol no MT usa base de 50%)
const base = (p.key === "etanol" && row.uf === "MT") ? row.pmpf * 0.5 : row.pmpf;
if (Math.abs(base * row.aliquota / 100 - row.estadual) > 0.0015) err.estadual = true;
// GNV: PIS/COFINS = PMPF × 9,25%
if (p.key === "gnv" && Math.abs(row.pmpf * 0.0925 - row.federal) > 0.0015) err.federal = true;

No Actions, se qualquer conta não fecha, o XML não é gravado — o aviso pede revisão humana no site, e as execuções seguintes tentam de novo. Uma alucinação nunca vira nota fiscal.

Economia de chamadas: se o XML do mês já existe em xml/, o site carrega direto; o resultado da IA fica salvo no navegador, então recarregar a página não chama o modelo de novo.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Sendo honesto: a parte de IA aqui não é aberta. Escolhi o Gemini porque o plano gratuito lê PDF com tabela em imagem de forma confiável, não exige cartão e o volume é mínimo (uma leitura por mês). Para um site estático sem servidor, isso resolveu.

Mas o projeto mostra exatamente onde um caminho fechado incomoda:

  • A chave fica exposta no index.html publicado (restrita por referenciador e API, mas ainda assim pública). Um modelo local não teria chave nenhuma.
  • Dependência de fornecedor: precisei de uma lista de fallbacks porque modelos somem ou mudam de nome. Um modelo open-weight com versão fixa daria a mesma resposta amanhã — algo valioso quando o resultado vai para documento fiscal.
  • Dados: no plano gratuito o Google pode usar o conteúdo enviado. Hoje só vai o PDF público da Fecombustíveis, então não há problema — mas eu não poderia fazer o mesmo com documentos de clientes.

O que é aberto: todo o código, o workflow, as regras de validação e o histórico de XMLs estão no GitHub, públicos. Qualquer posto, contador ou software fiscal pode copiar, auditar as contas ou usar os XMLs.

Próximo passo: como o prompt já pede JSON estrito e a validação aritmética independe do modelo, a troca é isolada numa função (chamarGemini). O plano é testar um modelo de visão open-weight (por exemplo, Gemma) rodando dentro do próprio GitHub Actions ou localmente e comparar a taxa de "contas que não fecham" com o Gemini.

The Spirit of It

No Día de los Muertos a gente lembra quem veio antes. No XML de tributos, nada é apagado: cada mês que passa vira um bloco com data de fim, e o novo começa no dia seguinte. Quando alguém abrir uma nota de setembro daqui a cinco anos, os valores de setembro ainda estarão lá.

E o fantasma? Ele aparece às 21h, 5h e 13h (horário de Brasília), olha a página, e na maioria das vezes vai embora em silêncio. Quando a tributação muda, ele deixa um recado no Discord. 👻

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot — a automação inteira (busca, geração do XML, publicação e avisos) roda em GitHub Actions.

articles.title: Three CSVs In, 1,272 Food Pages Out: PregNut's Boring Static Build
articles.description: PregNut is a free pregnancy food lookup I've been building since 2018. You search a food and see how...
articles.body_html:
PregNut is a free pregnancy food lookup I've been building since 2018. You search a food and see how 100 grams of it stacks up against the daily amounts pregnancy asks for. It has 1,272 foods and 13 nutrients, and each food gets its own page.

There's no database server behind it. It's an Eleventy site that builds from three CSV files and deploys to Cloudflare Pages. I like boring stacks for side projects, and this one has stayed easy to work on through three pregnancies, so here's how it fits together.

The inputs

The database/ folder has three files: FoodList.csv, NutrientList.csv and daily requirements.csv. The food list has the USDA NDB number, name, food group and a warning field. The nutrient list is long and skinny, one row per food per nutrient with a value and a unit. The requirements file has the daily reference amount for each nutrient as a label like "1000 mg" or "0.3 g."

All of it comes from a fixed snapshot of the USDA's SR Legacy data. USDA's final Standard Reference release was in 2018, so the numbers are frozen. For a reference site I count that as a feature. A value doesn't change under you between builds. The cost is that newer data and current product labels can differ, and the About page says that.

A tiny build script instead of a dependency

scripts/build-fooddata.js reads the CSVs and writes one JSON file the site uses everywhere. I wrote a minimal CSV parser for it, small enough to read in one sitting. It handles quoted fields and doubled quotes, and it strips a byte order mark if there is one. That BOM will quietly rename your first column header if you don't strip it.

The requirements file has a reference list under the main table, so the parser stops when it hits the SourceId row. Reference amounts get parsed with a small regex into a number and a unit.

One choice I'd make again. If the CSVs aren't present but the JSON already exists, the script prints a warning and keeps the existing JSON instead of failing. That lets a deploy work from the committed JSON alone.

One page per food with pagination

Eleventy's pagination does the heavy lifting. The food page template paginates over a data file with size: 1, so every item becomes its own page. The permalink is /food/{{ food.slug }}/, and the slug starts with the USDA number: /food/15151-shrimp-cooked/, /food/15152-shrimp-canned/. Food names repeat a lot in USDA data. The number keeps every URL unique without me thinking about it.

The data file is also where per-page decisions live. Title overrides for pages that get search traffic, related blog posts, and special cases. The human milk record, for example, stays in the dataset but is labeled as a historical data record only and left out of the food listings.

Units needed a helper. DHA is stored in grams and its benchmark is 0.3 g, while other nutrients are in mg or mcg. There's a small conversion function so comparisons always happen in the same unit.

Each page shows two columns: per 100 g, and a serving based on FDA reference amounts. Cooked shrimp shows 3 oz (85 g) next to 100 g. The 100 g column is for comparing foods. The serving column is closer to what's on a plate.

What the data can't do

The dataset has no iodine values. Rather than fake it, the site has an iodine guide and says the data is missing. Folate is shown as DFE, which isn't the same thing as the folic acid number on a prenatal label, so that gets its own guide too.

PregNut is an educational reference and isn't medical advice. Every page says so in the footer.

Deploys and one contact form

A GitHub Actions workflow runs npm run build and deploys with wrangler. Pushes to master go to pregnut.com. Pull requests get a preview deploy, and the link gets posted on the PR. Previews are only built for branches in the repo, and the actions are pinned to commit SHAs. The *.pages.dev hosts send X-Robots-Tag: noindex from _headers, so Google only indexes the real domain.

The one dynamic piece is /api/contact, a Cloudflare Pages Function. I wanted a free email relay and picked FormSubmit, which turned out to refuse requests coming from Workers. So the function does validation, a honeypot, a timing check and rate limiting, and only then hands the browser the relay endpoint to send to. Bots that fail the checks never see it.

If you want to see the output, open any food page on pregnut.com and view source. The numbers and the notes are right there in the HTML.
